questions.q:
A 70 kg fisherman from Massawa is diagnosed with hyperthyroidism caused by Graves' disease, and his basal metabolic rate is measured at 168 percent of the value expected for a healthy man of his age and body mass. His expected normal basal metabolic rate is 6800 kJ per day.
(a) Calculate his actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the excess energy in kJ per day that his body expends above the normal value.
(c) Express this excess as a percentage of the normal basal metabolic rate.
(d) Explain the endocrine basis of this raised metabolic rate and name the gland and the hormone responsible.
questions.answer: (a) 11,424 kJ per day; (b) 4624 kJ per day of excess expenditure; (c) 68 percent above the normal basal metabolic rate; (d) the thyroid gland is hypersecreting thyroxine, and because thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate, energy expenditure rises far above normal.
why: **Identify the given data and the principle.** Normal basal metabolic rate = 6800 kJ per day; measured rate = 168 percent of normal. Thyroxine is described in the unit as the primary regulator of basal metabolic rate, and hyperthyroidism accelerates metabolic rate to pathological levels.
**Calculate the actual basal metabolic rate.** Actual rate = 1.68 x 6800 kJ per day = 11,424 kJ per day.
**Calculate the excess expenditure.** Excess = 11,424 kJ per day - 6800 kJ per day = 4624 kJ per day.

**Express the excess as a percentage.** Percentage excess = (4624 / 6800) x 100 percent = 0.68 x 100 percent = 68 percent, which agrees with the measured value being 68 percent above the normal 100 percent.

**Explain the endocrine mechanism.** The gland responsible is the thyroid gland, which is hypersecreting thyroxine. Thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate and regulate heat production, so an excess of thyroxine raises oxygen and fuel consumption above normal. This explains the unit's clinical picture of hyperthyroidism: rapid weight loss despite eating, heat intolerance, hyperactive reflexes and anxiety, together with chronic strain on the cardiovascular system from elevated heart rate and blood pressure.

**State the final results.** (a) 11,424 kJ per day; (b) 4624 kJ per day in excess; (c) 68 percent above normal; (d) hypersecretion of thyroxine by the thyroid gland elevates the basal metabolic rate of most somatic cells.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
A 55 kg woman in Asmara with adult thyroxine hyposecretion has a basal metabolic rate measured at 82 percent of the value expected for a healthy woman of her age and body mass. Her expected normal rate is 5400 kJ per day.
(a) Calculate her actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the energy deficit in kJ per day relative to the normal value.
(c) Express this deficit as a percentage of the normal basal metabolic rate.
(d) Name the hormone that is deficient and explain why this reduces her basal metabolic rate.
questions.answer: (a) 4428 kJ per day; (b) 972 kJ per day below normal; (c) 18 percent below normal; (d) thyroxine is deficient, and since thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate and regulate heat production, its shortage lowers metabolism, matching the sluggish metabolism, weight gain and cold sensitivity of myxoedema.
why: **Convert the percentage to a multiplier.** A rate at 82 percent of normal corresponds to a multiplying factor of 0.82 applied to the normal value of 5400 kJ per day.
**Calculate the actual rate.** 0.82 x 5400 kJ per day = 4428 kJ per day.
**Calculate the deficit.** Deficit = 5400 kJ per day - 4428 kJ per day = 972 kJ per day.
**Express the deficit as a percentage.** (972 / 5400) x 100 percent = 18 percent, consistent with 100 percent - 82 percent = 18 percent.

**Explain the endocrine cause.** The deficient hormone is thyroxine, the primary regulator of basal metabolic rate. With less thyroxine acting on most somatic cells, heat production and metabolic rate fall, producing the low metabolic rate, weight gain and cold sensitivity characteristic of myxoedema.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q:
A 16-year-old boy in Keren with a pituitary tumour has a basal metabolic rate measured at 120 percent of the normal value for his age and body mass, his normal rate being 6000 kJ per day. The tumour is hypersecreting Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH).
(a) Calculate his actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the excess energy expended per day.
(c) Express the excess as a percentage of the normal rate.
(d) Explain the full chain of events from the pituitary tumour to the raised metabolic rate.
questions.answer: (a) 7200 kJ per day; (b) 1200 kJ per day in excess; (c) 20 percent above normal; (d) excess TSH from the tumour over-stimulates the thyroid gland, which synthesizes and releases excess thyroxine; thyroxine then acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate, raising energy expenditure by 20 percent.
why: **Calculate the actual rate.** 1.20 x 6000 kJ per day = 7200 kJ per day.
**Calculate the excess.** Excess = 7200 kJ per day - 6000 kJ per day = 1200 kJ per day.
**Express the excess as a percentage.** (1200 / 6000) x 100 percent = 20 percent, consistent with 120 percent - 100 percent = 20 percent.

**Trace the hormonal chain.** TSH has the thyroid gland as its principal target tissue and stimulates the synthesis and release of thyroxine, so a TSH-secreting pituitary tumour drives thyroxine secretion upward.

**Link thyroxine to metabolism.** Thyroxine's target is most somatic cells, where it elevates the basal metabolic rate and regulates heat production; the excess hormone therefore accounts for the measured 20 percent rise in energy expenditure.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Which hormone is NOT made by the anterior pituitary?
why: Step 1: list the anterior six — FLAT PG: FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, Prolactin, GH.
Step 2: oxytocin is not in the list.
Step 3: oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior lobe.
questions.tip: Write “FLAT PG” in the margin before answering any pituitary question.

similar.q: Which two hormones does the posterior pituitary release?

questions.label: 1.1.1 Practice — pituitary

questions.q: ADH acts on the
why: Step 1: ADH = antidiuretic = “against much urine”.
Step 2: water is saved by reabsorbing it in the kidney.
Step 3: the collecting ducts become more permeable → more water returns to the blood.
questions.tip: Target of ADH is always the kidney (tubules / collecting ducts).

similar.q: What happens to urine volume when ADH rises?
similar.a: It falls and the urine becomes more concentrated.

questions.label: 1.1.1 Practice — pituitary

questions.q: Distinguish gigantism from acromegaly.
questions.answer: Both are caused by too much growth hormone. Gigantism happens in childhood (before the long bones stop growing) — the person becomes very tall with normal proportions. Acromegaly happens in adults — the bones can no longer lengthen, so the bones of the face, hands and feet thicken and enlarge.
why: Step 1: same hormone — excess GH.
Step 2: different age — child vs adult.
Step 3: different result — long bones lengthen (tall) vs flat/end bones thicken (big jaw, hands, feet).
questions.tip: Age decides the disease: child = gigantism, adult = acromegaly.

similar.q: What does too little GH in childhood cause?
similar.a: Pituitary dwarfism — short but proportionate, normal intelligence.

questions.label: 1.1.1 Practice — pituitary

questions.q: ADH is also called ____ because at high concentration it narrows blood vessels.
why: Step 1: vaso = vessel, pressin = press/squeeze.
Step 2: narrowing vessels raises blood pressure → vasopressin.
questions.tip: Split the word into its parts: vaso-pressin.

similar.q: What is another name for growth hormone?

questions.label: 1.1.1 Practice — pituitary

questions.q: The posterior pituitary makes ADH and oxytocin.
why: Step 1: the posterior lobe has no hormone-making cells.
Step 2: neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus make ADH and oxytocin.
Step 3: the posterior lobe only stores and releases them → false.
questions.tip: Watch the verb: “makes/produces/synthesises” vs “stores/releases”.

similar.q: True or false: the anterior lobe makes its own hormones.

questions.label: 1.1.1 Practice — pituitary

questions.q: FSH in males stimulates

options.B: sperm production in the seminiferous tubules

why: Step 1: FSH = follicle-stimulating in females.
Step 2: its male job is the “sperm factory” — seminiferous tubules.
Step 3: LH (not FSH) acts on Leydig cells.
questions.tip: FSH → Factory of sperm / Follicle. LH → Leydig cells / Luteum.

similar.q: In females, what does LH stimulate after ovulation?
similar.a: The corpus luteum to secrete progesterone.

questions.label: 1.1.1 Practice — pituitary

questions.q: Explain why a person under the influence of alcohol produces a lot of dilute urine (Review Part I Q8).
questions.answer: Alcohol inhibits the release of ADH from the posterior pituitary. With little ADH, the collecting ducts reabsorb little water, so a large volume of dilute urine is produced and the person becomes dehydrated.
why: Step 1: normal role of ADH — water reabsorption.
Step 2: alcohol blocks ADH release.
Step 3: less water reabsorbed → more dilute urine → thirst, dehydration.
questions.tip: Any “more urine” question: think first of ADH falling.

similar.q: How does hypersecretion of ADH affect urine?

questions.label: 1.1.1 Practice — pituitary

questions.q: Over-secretion of prolactin in a woman who is not breastfeeding may cause
why: Step 1: prolactin → milk.
Step 2: too much → milk at the wrong time, menstrual periods stop, infertility (textbook p.18).
questions.tip: Prolactin excess = “milk + no periods”.

similar.q: What does prolactin excess cause in males?

questions.label: 1.1.1 Practice — pituitary

questions.q: Oxytocin is said to work by positive feedback during childbirth. Explain.
questions.answer: Stretching of the cervix by the baby’s head sends impulses to the hypothalamus → more oxytocin is released → stronger uterine contractions push the baby further → more stretching → even more oxytocin. The cycle grows until the baby is born and the stretching stops.
why: Step 1: stimulus — stretch of the cervix.
Step 2: response — oxytocin → contractions.
Step 3: the response increases the stimulus (more stretch) → the loop amplifies.
Step 4: it ends with birth.
questions.tip: Negative feedback reverses a change; positive feedback makes it bigger.

similar.q: Give one example of negative feedback in the pituitary.
similar.a: High thyroxine reduces TSH; dilute blood stops ADH release.

questions.label: 1.1.1 Practice — pituitary

questions.q: The thyroid gland is located

options.B: at the base of the neck in front of the trachea

why: Step 1: butterfly-shaped gland in the neck.
Step 2: it wraps the front of the trachea (windpipe).
questions.tip: Thyroid → throat.

similar.q: Where are the parathyroid glands?
similar.a: Behind the thyroid gland, usually four.

questions.label: 1.1.2 Practice — thyroid

questions.q: Under-secretion of thyroxine in childhood causes ____.
why: Step 1: under-secretion = hypothyroidism.
Step 2: child → cretinism; adult → myxoedema.
questions.tip: C for Child and Cretinism.

similar.q: Under-secretion of thyroxine in an adult causes ____.

questions.label: 1.1.2 Practice — thyroid

questions.q: Explain how negative feedback keeps the thyroxine level constant.
questions.answer: When the thyroxine level rises too high, it acts on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, which then release less TRH and TSH. With less TSH the thyroid releases less thyroxine, so the level falls back to normal. When thyroxine is low, more TRH and TSH are released and the thyroid secretes more.
why: Step 1: chain — TRH → TSH → thyroxine.
Step 2: high thyroxine switches the top of the chain off.
Step 3: thyroxine falls → normal.
Step 4: low thyroxine releases the brake → more TSH.
questions.tip: Always draw the three-box loop and add a dashed “−” arrow back to the top.

similar.q: In a goitre caused by iodine lack, is TSH high or low?
similar.a: High — there is not enough thyroxine to switch it off.

questions.label: 1.1.2 Practice — thyroid

questions.q: Which is a sign of hyperthyroidism?

options.B: Weight loss, sweating and fast heartbeat

why: Step 1: hyper = too much thyroxine = metabolic rate high.
Step 2: high rate burns food (weight loss), makes heat (sweating) and speeds the heart.
Step 3: the other options are hypothyroid signs.
questions.tip: Hyper = Hot, Thin, Fast. Hypo = Slow, Cold, Fat, Tired.

similar.q: Name two signs of myxoedema.
similar.a: Puffy swollen face, low metabolic rate, weight gain, sensitivity to cold, sluggishness.

questions.label: 1.1.2 Practice — thyroid

questions.q: Calcitonin raises the level of calcium in the blood.
why: Step 1: calcitonin is released when blood calcium is high.
Step 2: it moves calcium into bone → blood calcium falls.
Step 3: PTH is the hormone that raises it → false.
questions.tip: Calci-TONE-in tones it down.

similar.q: Which gland secretes the hormone that raises blood calcium?

questions.label: 1.1.2 Practice — thyroid

questions.q: Why does eating iodised salt prevent goitre?
questions.answer: Iodine is a component of thyroxine. With enough iodine the thyroid can make normal amounts of thyroxine, which gives negative feedback to the pituitary, so TSH does not stay high and the gland does not enlarge.
why: Step 1: iodine → thyroxine.
Step 2: normal thyroxine → feedback → normal TSH.
Step 3: no over-stimulation → no swelling.
questions.tip: Connect three things: iodine, thyroxine, TSH.

similar.q: Which other food is rich in iodine?
similar.a: Sea food (fish, seaweed) — e.g. from the Red Sea coast.

questions.label: 1.1.2 Practice — thyroid

questions.q: Thyroxine is chemically
why: Step 1: thyroxine is made from the amino acid tyrosine.
Step 2: iodine atoms are attached → iodinated amine.
questions.tip: Thyroxine = tyrosine + iodine.

similar.q: Which hormone in the thyroid is a peptide?

questions.label: 1.1.2 Practice — thyroid

questions.q: Give three functions of thyroxine.
questions.answer: It controls the metabolic rate of the body; it regulates bone growth; it controls the development of the brain and nervous system in children (and metamorphosis in amphibians).
why: Step 1: metabolism — energy and heat.
Step 2: growth — bones.
Step 3: development — brain in children; tadpole to frog.
questions.tip: Remember “Metabolism, Growth, Brain”.

similar.q: Which disorder shows that thyroxine is needed for brain development?

questions.label: 1.1.2 Practice — thyroid

questions.q: The outer part of the adrenal gland is the ____.
why: Step 1: cortex = bark/outer layer.
Step 2: medulla = inner core.
questions.tip: Cortex = Coat (outside).

similar.q: Which part of the adrenal gland receives nerve impulses?

questions.label: 1.1.4 Practice — adrenal

questions.q: Which group of hormones is secreted by the adrenal cortex?
why: Step 1: cortex hormones are steroids called corticosteroids (corticoids).
Step 2: three groups — glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, sex steroids.
questions.tip: Cortex → corticosteroids (same root).

similar.q: Name the major glucocorticoid.

questions.label: 1.1.4 Practice — adrenal

questions.q: Aldosterone is secreted in response to low blood sodium and high potassium. State its effect on the kidney and on the blood.
questions.answer: It makes the kidney tubules reabsorb more sodium and excrete more potassium. Water follows the sodium, so blood sodium, blood volume and blood pressure rise back to normal while extra potassium is removed.
why: Step 1: stimulus — low Na⁺, high K⁺.
Step 2: action — keep Na⁺, lose K⁺.
Step 3: water follows Na⁺ → blood volume restored.
questions.tip: Aldosterone = “salt keeper”; ADH = “water keeper”.

similar.q: Which disease includes a lack of aldosterone?

questions.label: 1.1.4 Practice — adrenal

questions.q: Which is NOT an effect of adrenaline?

options.C: Blood diverted to the gut for digestion

why: Step 1: adrenaline prepares for fight or flight.
Step 2: blood is sent to muscles; digestion is slowed.
Step 3: so “blood to the gut” is the wrong one.
questions.tip: Ask: “Would this help me run from danger right now?”

similar.q: Which hormone is mainly responsible for constricting blood vessels throughout the body?

questions.label: 1.1.4 Practice — adrenal

questions.q: The adrenal glands are located on top of the kidneys.
why: Step 1: ad = near, renal = kidney.
Step 2: one sits above each kidney → true.
questions.tip: The name tells the address.

similar.q: What colour are the adrenal glands?

questions.label: 1.1.4 Practice — adrenal

questions.q: Distinguish Cushing’s disease from Addison’s disease.
questions.answer: Cushing’s disease is caused by hypersecretion of glucocorticoids (cortisol): weakness, high blood pressure, bruises, high blood sugar. Addison’s disease is caused by hyposecretion of glucocorticoids and aldosterone (failure of the adrenal cortex): anorexia, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, low blood glucose, muscular weakness and bronzing of the skin.
why: Step 1: both are adrenal cortex disorders.
Step 2: Cushing = too much; Addison = too little.
Step 3: list two signs of each.
questions.tip: Cushing = Cushion (too much, round). Addison = Adds nothing (too little).

similar.q: What happens with over-secretion of adrenaline?
similar.a: Tumour of the medulla with high blood pressure, severe headache, sweating and faintness.

questions.label: 1.1.4 Practice — adrenal

questions.q: Emotions such as fear and anger increase the secretion of
why: Step 1: fear → nerve impulses → adrenal medulla.
Step 2: medulla → epinephrine (adrenaline).
questions.tip: Fear = fight or flight = epinephrine.

similar.q: Why is the adrenal sometimes called the “emergency gland”?
similar.a: Its medulla releases adrenaline that prepares the body for immediate action in an emergency.

questions.label: 1.1.4 Practice — adrenal

questions.q: Explain why the adrenal gland is described as “two glands in one”.
questions.answer: The outer cortex and the inner medulla differ in structure, hormones and control. The cortex secretes steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, sex steroids) under the control of ACTH and blood salts; the medulla secretes amines (adrenaline, noradrenaline) when it receives nerve impulses.
why: Step 1: structure — outer vs inner.
Step 2: hormones — steroids vs amines.
Step 3: control — hormones/salts vs nerves.
questions.tip: Compare three things: position, hormones, control.

similar.q: Which part is essential for life?
similar.a: The cortex (without aldosterone and cortisol, salt balance and blood sugar fail).

questions.label: 1.1.4 Practice — adrenal

questions.q: The islets of Langerhans are found in the
why: Step 1: islets = small islands of endocrine cells.
Step 2: they are scattered through the pancreas.
questions.tip: Islets → pancreas.

similar.q: Which islet cells secrete insulin?

questions.label: 1.1.5 Practice — pancreas

questions.q: Explain how insulin and glucagon regulate blood glucose (Review Part IV Q2).
questions.answer: When blood glucose rises above normal, β-cells release insulin, which makes the liver and muscles take up glucose and convert it into glycogen, and cells use more glucose, so the level falls. When it falls below normal, α-cells release glucagon, which makes the liver convert glycogen into glucose and release it, so the level rises. They act antagonistically to keep about 100 mg/100 cm³.
why: Step 1: high glucose → insulin → store as glycogen → falls.
Step 2: low glucose → glucagon → glycogen to glucose → rises.
Step 3: opposite actions = antagonistic; controlled by negative feedback.
questions.tip: Write two arrows: high → insulin → down; low → glucagon → up.

similar.q: Why must insulin be injected rather than swallowed?
similar.a: It is a protein and would be digested in the stomach and intestine.

questions.label: 1.1.5 Practice — pancreas

questions.q: Failure of insulin secretion causes diabetes ____.
why: Step 1: insulin → glucose control.
Step 2: glucose in urine = “mellitus” (sweet).
questions.tip: Mellitus = honey (sugar). Insipidus = no taste (ADH).

similar.q: Lack of which hormone causes diabetes insipidus?

questions.label: 1.1.5 Practice — pancreas

questions.q: A diabetic person usually has

options.A: glucose in the urine and frequent thirst
options.B: very dilute urine with no glucose
options.C: low blood glucose all the time

why: Step 1: no insulin → blood glucose high.
Step 2: kidneys cannot reabsorb it all → glucose in urine.
Step 3: water lost with glucose → thirst and much urine.
questions.tip: Glucose in urine is the key clue for diabetes mellitus.

similar.q: Why do untreated diabetics lose weight?
similar.a: Cells cannot use glucose, so fats and proteins are broken down for energy.

questions.label: 1.1.5 Practice — pancreas

questions.q: Glucagon converts glucose into glycogen.
why: Step 1: glucagon raises blood glucose.
Step 2: it does this by changing glycogen INTO glucose.
Step 3: insulin is the one that makes glycogen → false.
questions.tip: GlucaGON: glucose GONE → bring it back from glycogen.

similar.q: True or false: insulin lowers blood sugar.

questions.label: 1.1.5 Practice — pancreas

questions.q: Describe the exocrine and endocrine functions of the pancreas.
questions.answer: Exocrine: most pancreatic cells secrete pancreatic juice containing digestive enzymes, which flows through the pancreatic duct into the duodenum. Endocrine: the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin (β-cells) and glucagon (α-cells) directly into the blood to control blood glucose.
why: Step 1: exocrine → duct → digestive juice.
Step 2: endocrine → no duct → hormones into blood.
questions.tip: Name the product and where it goes for each part.

similar.q: Name another organ that is both exocrine and endocrine.

questions.label: 1.1.5 Practice — pancreas

questions.q: Immediately after a meal rich in carbohydrate, the hormone whose secretion increases is
why: Step 1: digested sugar raises blood glucose.
Step 2: high glucose → β-cells → insulin.
questions.tip: Food in → insulin up.

similar.q: Which hormone rises during a long fast?

questions.label: 1.1.5 Practice — pancreas

questions.q: Why is it dangerous for a diabetic to eat a diet with a lot of sugar?
questions.answer: The sugar is absorbed into the blood, but without (enough) insulin it cannot be taken up by cells or stored as glycogen. Blood glucose rises even higher; very high levels can damage brain cells and cause coma or death.
why: Step 1: sugar → blood glucose rises.
Step 2: no insulin → cannot be stored or used.
Step 3: very high glucose → coma risk.
questions.tip: Answer with cause → effect → danger.

similar.q: What is hypoglycaemia and what can cause it in a diabetic?
similar.a: Abnormally low blood glucose — for example after too much insulin or missing a meal.

questions.label: 1.1.5 Practice — pancreas

questions.q: The endocrine tissue of the testes is the
why: Step 1: tubules make sperm.
Step 2: Leydig cells between them make testosterone.
questions.tip: Leydig = Lets out testosterone (under LH).

similar.q: Which pituitary hormone stimulates Leydig cells?

questions.label: 1.1.6 Practice — sex glands

questions.q: The corpus luteum secretes ____.
why: Step 1: corpus luteum forms from the empty follicle after ovulation.
Step 2: under LH it secretes progesterone.
questions.tip: Luteum ↔ LH ↔ progesterone.

similar.q: Which hormone does the growing follicle secrete?

questions.label: 1.1.6 Practice — sex glands

questions.q: List four male secondary sexual characteristics caused by testosterone.
questions.answer: Deepening of the voice, growth of beard and body hair, increased muscle development, broadening of the chest and shoulders (also enlargement of the testes and sperm production).
why: Step 1: voice.
Step 2: hair.
Step 3: muscles.
Step 4: body shape.
questions.tip: Use a head-to-body order: voice, beard, chest, muscles.

similar.q: List two female secondary sexual characteristics.
similar.a: Breast enlargement and broadening of the hips.

questions.label: 1.1.6 Practice — sex glands

questions.q: Sex hormones are protein hormones.
why: Step 1: testosterone, oestrogen and progesterone are made from cholesterol.
Step 2: they are steroids → false.
questions.tip: Endings -sterone and -gen (oestrogen) here = steroid.

similar.q: Name a protein hormone that controls the gonads.

questions.label: 1.1.6 Practice — sex glands

questions.q: Which statement about the ovary is correct?

options.B: It produces ova and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone

why: Step 1: gonads have two jobs — gametes and hormones.
Step 2: ovary → ova + oestrogen + progesterone.
Step 3: FSH comes from the pituitary.
questions.tip: Gonad = gametes + sex hormones.

similar.q: Why are gonads called mixed glands?
similar.a: They release gametes (exocrine-like) and hormones into blood (endocrine).

questions.label: 1.1.6 Practice — sex glands

questions.q: Explain how the hypothalamus and pituitary control the secretion of sex hormones (Review Part II Q3).
questions.answer: The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which makes the anterior pituitary secrete FSH and LH. These stimulate the testes (sperm and testosterone) or ovaries (follicle growth, oestrogen; corpus luteum, progesterone). High levels of sex hormones feed back to reduce GnRH, FSH and LH.
why: Step 1: GnRH.
Step 2: FSH + LH.
Step 3: gonad hormones.
Step 4: negative feedback.
questions.tip: Draw the loop: brain → pituitary → gonad → back.

similar.q: Why does the combined contraceptive pill stop ovulation?
similar.a: Its oestrogen/progesterone give negative feedback, keeping FSH and LH low.

questions.label: 1.1.6 Practice — sex glands

questions.q: Puberty begins because

options.B: the hypothalamus becomes less sensitive to androgens and releases more GnRH

why: Step 1: before puberty small amounts of androgens inhibit GnRH.
Step 2: at puberty the hypothalamus becomes less sensitive → more GnRH → more FSH and LH (textbook p.38).
questions.tip: Puberty starts in the brain, not in the gonads.

similar.q: Which hormone rises first at puberty: GnRH or testosterone?

questions.label: 1.1.6 Practice — sex glands

questions.q: A woman’s ovaries stop working at menopause. Predict the levels of oestrogen and FSH, and explain.
questions.answer: Oestrogen falls because there are almost no follicles to make it. FSH (and LH) rise, because low oestrogen no longer gives negative feedback to the hypothalamus and pituitary.
why: Step 1: no follicles → little oestrogen.
Step 2: less negative feedback → more GnRH → more FSH, LH.
questions.tip: When a gland fails, its own hormone falls but the pituitary hormone that drives it rises.

similar.q: What happens to TSH when the thyroid fails?

questions.label: 1.1.6 Practice — sex glands

questions.q: The thymus gland is found

options.A: in the neck behind the thyroid
options.B: in the chest behind the sternum, below the thyroid

why: Step 1: thymus — central chest cavity.
Step 2: below the thyroid, behind the breastbone, above the heart.
questions.tip: Thymus = thorax (chest).

similar.q: Which endocrine gland is inside the brain and light-sensitive?

questions.label: 1.1.7 Practice — thymus

questions.q: The thymus secretes the hormone ____.
why: Step 1: thymus → thymosin (same root).
Step 2: thyroxine is from the thyroid — do not mix them.
questions.tip: Thym-osin ↔ Thym-us; Thyr-oxine ↔ Thyr-oid.

similar.q: Which gland secretes melatonin?

questions.label: 1.1.7 Practice — thymus

questions.q: The thymus gland grows larger in adults than in children.
why: Step 1: it is relatively large in newborns and children.
Step 2: it shrinks after puberty and nearly disappears in adults → false.
questions.tip: Thymus = childhood gland.

similar.q: What tissue replaces the thymus in adults?

questions.label: 1.1.7 Practice — thymus

questions.q: State the function of thymosin and explain why it is important.
questions.answer: Thymosin stimulates the production and maturation of T lymphocytes (T cells), white blood cells that multiply, differentiate and mature in the thymus and then defend the body against pathogens. Without them the body has weak immunity and suffers frequent infections.
why: Step 1: thymosin → T cells.
Step 2: T cells → immunity.
Step 3: no T cells → infections.
questions.tip: Function + reason = full marks.

similar.q: Which virus attacks a type of T cell?
similar.a: HIV (it attacks helper T cells, causing AIDS).

questions.label: 1.1.7 Practice — thymus

questions.q: The thymus is functional primarily during
why: Step 1: it is largest and most active in childhood.
Step 2: after puberty it degenerates.
questions.tip: Think “T-cell school is open in childhood”.

similar.q: After which stage of life does the thymus shrink sharply?

questions.label: 1.1.7 Practice — thymus

questions.q: Which gland is matched correctly?

options.B: Thymus — plays a role in immunity

why: Step 1: thymus → thymosin → T cells.
Step 2: T cells → immunity.
Step 3: the other jobs belong to parathyroids, adrenal cortex and thyroid.
questions.tip: Match by the hormone first, then the job.

similar.q: Which gland matches “hormones that need iodine for secretion”?

questions.label: 1.1.7 Practice — thymus

questions.q: Why does removing the thymus from a newborn animal weaken its immunity much more than removing it from an adult?
questions.answer: In the newborn, T cells have not yet matured; without the thymus (thymosin) they never develop, so immunity fails. In the adult, most T cells have already been produced and continue to work, so removal has little effect.
why: Step 1: thymus works mostly early in life.
Step 2: newborn — no T cells will mature.
Step 3: adult — T cells already made.
questions.tip: Age is the key word in thymus questions.

similar.q: Why is the thymus large in children?
similar.a: Because most T cells are being produced and trained during childhood.

questions.label: 1.1.7 Practice — thymus

questions.q: Compare the thymus and the thyroid: location, hormone and function.
questions.answer: Thymus: in the chest behind the sternum; thymosin; T-cell maturation (immunity). Thyroid: base of the neck in front of the trachea; thyroxine and calcitonin; metabolic rate, growth and blood calcium.
why: Step 1: location.
Step 2: hormone.
Step 3: function.
questions.tip: Use a three-column table when asked to compare.

similar.q: Which of the two needs iodine?

questions.label: 1.1.7 Practice — thymus

units.title: The Reproductive System
units.intro: **Primary** characters = the gonads and genitalia you are born with. **Secondary** = puberty changes (voice, hair, breasts, hips) driven by sex hormones.

cards.title: 2.1 Primary and Secondary Sexual Characteristics
body: **Reproduction** is a biological process in which new individuals are produced from their parent(s).
Reproduction is important in ensuring the continuity of life and/or the species.
Reproduction also increases the number of individuals of a species.
In asexual reproduction only one parent produces offspring of the same genetic makeup.
Part or parts of an organism break off to produce more of the same kind, or the organism divides into two or more parts.

cards.title: Key table
head: Anatomical Structure
Primary Secretions / Cell Types
Physiological Role in Male Reproduction
rows: Site of spermatogenesis and physical support of germ cells
Interstitial cells that synthesize androgens under $$LH$$ control
Stores spermatozoa and facilitates biochemical maturation of motility
Secretes the bulk of semen volume, providing energy and uterine motility
Neutralizes vaginal acidity and liquefies semen after ejaculation
Cleanses and neutralizes the urethra prior to semen passage

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following is considered a primary male sexual characteristic?

steps.text: **Step 1: Define primary sexual characteristics**
Primary sexual characteristics refer to the anatomical structures directly involved in reproduction that are present at birth.
**Step 2: Identify from options**
Testes and the penis are reproductive organs present at birth.
Deep voice, broad shoulders, and facial hair are secondary sexual characteristics that emerge during puberty.

cards.answer: The presence of the testes and penis

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: The scrotum maintains the temperature of the testes at which of the following ranges relative to core body temperature?

steps.text: **Step 1: Understand testicular temperature requirements**
Viable spermatogenesis requires a temperature slightly lower than the core body temperature of $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.
**Step 2: Identify the scrotum function**
The scrotum is situated outside the pelvic cavity, cooling the testes by approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core body temperature.
**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which cells in the interstitial tissue of the testes produce the androgen testosterone?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify cell types in the testes**
Seminiferous tubules contain spermatogonia and Sertoli cells. The interstitial spaces between the tubules contain Leydig cells.

**Step 2: Match with hormone function**
Leydig cells produce androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Leydig cells**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the function of the acrosome located at the head of a mature sperm cell?

options.A: To pack mitochondria for metabolic energy
options.B: To contain hydrolytic enzymes to penetrate the egg membranes
options.C: To provide motility for the sperm cell
options.D: To store glycogen for long-term survival

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand sperm head anatomy**
The head of the sperm contains the nucleus and is capped by the acrosome.

**Step 2: Define acrosome function**
The acrosome contains digestive enzymes that dissolve the outer layers of the secondary oocyte during fertilization.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **To contain hydrolytic enzymes to penetrate the egg membranes**.

cards.title: Puberty and sexual characters
body: **Primary sexual characters** are the reproductive organs present at birth (testes or ovaries). **Secondary sexual characters** develop at puberty under hormones: in boys (testosterone): deeper voice, facial and body hair, broader shoulders, bigger muscles; in girls (oestrogen): breasts develop, hips widen, menstruation begins, body hair grows.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: **Seminal vesicles** secretes:

options.A: Mucous - like fluid that lubricate the end of penis
options.B: Milky fluid that neutralizes the byproducts of the sperm

cards.why: The **seminal vesicles** produce about 60% of the volume of semen. This fluid is **alkaline** (to neutralize vaginal acidity) and contains fructose (energy for sperm) and **prostaglandins** (to stimulate contractions in the female reproductive tract).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: During oogenesis, the unequal division of cytoplasm results in the production of which of the following?

options.B: One diploid zygote and three polar bodies
options.C: One functional haploid secondary oocyte and a non-functional polar body

cards.why:
**Step 1: Examine oogenesis division**
In meiosis I, the primary oocyte divides unequally.

**Step 2: Identify the products**
It yields one large haploid secondary oocyte (retaining most of the cytoplasm and nutrients) and one small, non-functional first polar body.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **One functional haploid secondary oocyte and a non-functional polar body**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: During oogenesis, the unequal division of cytoplasm results in the production of which of the following?

steps.text: **Step 1: Examine oogenesis division**
In meiosis I, the primary oocyte divides unequally.
**Step 2: Identify the products**
It yields one large haploid secondary oocyte (retaining most of the cytoplasm and nutrients) and one small, non-functional first polar body.
**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **One functional haploid secondary oocyte and a non-functional polar body**.

cards.answer: One functional haploid secondary oocyte and a non-functional polar body

cards.title: 2.2 The male reproductive system — organ by organ
body: **What the system must do.** The male system has three jobs: (1) **make sperm cells** (male gametes), (2) **deliver them into the female tract**, and (3) **make the male sex hormone testosterone**.
**The nine organs to know** (textbook p.28): **testes, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, Cowper’s glands, scrotum, penis.** Group them so they are easy to remember:
**① Primary sex organs (gonads)** — the two **testes**: make sperm and testosterone.
**② Ducts (tubes)** — **epididymis → vas deferens → urethra**: store, mature and carry sperm.
**③ Accessory glands** — **seminal vesicles, prostate, Cowper’s glands**: add the fluid part of semen.
**④ External organs** — **scrotum** (holds and cools the testes) and **penis** (places semen in the vagina).

**Primary vs secondary characters:** the genital organs above are **primary sexual characters** (present at birth). Changes at puberty — deep voice, beard, broad shoulders — are **secondary sexual characters** caused by testosterone.

cards.title: Follow one sperm: the route out of the body

steps.text: **Testis** — sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules.
**Epididymis** — hundreds of millions are stored and matured; they learn to swim.
**Vas deferens** (sperm duct) — muscular tube carries sperm up and round the bladder.
**Glands add fluid** — seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper’s glands; sperm + fluid = semen.
**Urethra** in the penis — semen leaves the body during ejaculation.

cards.title: The testes — where sperm and testosterone are made
body: **Shape and size:** two **oval (ovoid)** organs, about **5 cm long and 3 cm wide**. Each hangs from a **spermatic cord** (carrying blood vessels, nerves and the vas deferens) inside the sac-like **scrotum**.
**Why outside the body?** Body temperature (37 °C) is **too high** for normal sperm production. Sperm form best at **3–5 °C below** body temperature, so the testes hang outside the abdominal cavity.
**How they got there:** in the unborn baby the testes form inside the abdomen. **Testosterone**, secreted by the developing testes, makes them **descend into the scrotum**, usually before birth.

**Inside a testis:** it is packed with **highly coiled seminiferous tubules** (if stretched out, several hundred metres). The cells lining the inside of the tubules divide actively in mature males to make sperm (**spermatogenesis**).

**Between the tubules** are the **interstitial (Leydig) cells**, which secrete **testosterone** when stimulated by **LH**. Inside the tubules, nurse (**Sertoli**) cells feed the developing sperm (extra detail).
**So the testis is a mixed gland:** sperm leave through ducts (exocrine-like), testosterone goes into the blood (endocrine) — exactly what you met in 1.1.6.

cards.title: Spermatogenesis — how a sperm is made, step by step
body: **Step 1 — the stock.** Germ cells called **spermatogonia** are formed during **fetal life** and stored in the walls of the seminiferous tubules.
**Step 2 — the start.** At **puberty**, FSH (and testosterone) switch the tubules on. Spermatogonia divide by **mitosis** to keep up their numbers.

**Step 3 — halving the chromosomes.** Some cells grow into **primary spermatocytes** and divide by **meiosis**: 46 chromosomes → **23** in each **spermatid**. This is why a sperm carries only half the father’s genes.
**Step 4 — shaping.** Each round spermatid changes shape — grows a tail, packs its mitochondria, forms an acrosome — and becomes a **spermatozoon** (sperm).

**Step 5 — finishing school.** Sperm move to the **epididymis** to be stored and mature. The whole process takes about **two months**, and a healthy man makes **millions every day** from puberty to old age.
**Exam definition:** spermatogenesis is **the process of sperm cell formation** in the seminiferous tubules of the testes.

cards.title: Structure of the sperm cell — part by part

steps.text: **Head** — oval; holds a large **nucleus** with the father’s genetic material (23 chromosomes). Its front cap, the **acrosome**, contains **dissolving enzymes** to get through the coats of the ovum.
**Middle piece** — packed with **mitochondria**, which release energy (respiration) to drive the tail.
**Tail (flagellum)** — long and whip-like; lashes from side to side to **swim** through the uterus to the fallopian tube.
Sperm cells are among the **smallest** human cells, yet they must carry the father’s traits to the child.

cards.title: Sperm parts and how each is adapted
head: Part
Contains
Function
Adaptation idea
rows: Enzymes ready at the very tip
Mitochondria spiral round the tail base
Long whip pushes the cell forward

cards.title: Male path
body: Testis (sperm + testosterone) → epididymis → vas deferens → urethra. Glands (seminal vesicles, prostate, Cowper’s) add fluid. Sperm need a bag 3–5 °C cooler than the body — that is why the testes hang outside.

cards.title: The ducts — epididymis, vas deferens, urethra
body: **Epididymis:** a long, tightly coiled tube formed by the **union of the seminiferous tubules**; it lies in close contact with the **outer surface of each testis**. Here **hundreds of millions of sperm are temporarily stored and matured**. The epididymis and tubules make secretions in which the sperm live and move.

**Vas deferens (sperm duct):** one from each epididymis. They run up into the body, loop over the bladder, **join together and open into the urethra**. Their muscular walls squeeze sperm along during ejaculation. (Cutting and tying them is **vasectomy**, a permanent family-planning method — semen still forms, but contains no sperm.)
**Urethra:** a **common tube** running through the centre of the penis. Both **urine and semen** pass through it — but **never at the same time**: during ejaculation a muscle closes the bladder neck.
**If sperm are not released** they break down and are **absorbed by the male’s body** (Exercise 2.2 Q1).

cards.title: The three accessory glands — what each adds to semen
head: Gland
Secretion
Why it helps sperm
rows: Slightly **alkaline** fluid with **prostaglandins** (and fructose sugar — extra)
Regulates pH; prostaglandins make the female tract **contract**, helping sperm move towards the ovum; sugar = fuel
**Neutralises** the acidic sperm fluid (acid from wastes of stored sperm) and the acid of the vagina
**Lubricates** the end of the penis before intercourse

cards.title: Semen and ejaculation
body: **Semen** = sperm + secretions of the seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper’s glands. It is a **creamy-white suspension** that contains sperm **plus food and enzymes that make the sperm active**.

**Functions of the seminal fluid** (Exercise 2.2 Q3): (1) a **liquid medium** in which sperm swim; (2) **food** (sugar) for energy; (3) **alkali** to neutralise acids that would kill sperm; (4) **enzymes** that activate sperm; (5) **prostaglandins** that help sperm reach the ovum; (6) lubrication.
**Ejaculation:** a series of muscular **contractions** squeezes semen from the vas deferens and glands through the urethra and out of its **external opening**.

cards.title: Scrotum and penis — the external organs
body: **Scrotum:** a skin pouch that holds the **testes, the lower part of the spermatic cords and the epididymides**. It lies outside the body, behind the penis and in front of the upper thighs.

**The scrotum is a thermostat** (Do you know? p.31): normally its muscles are **relaxed** and the testes hang **away** from the warm body. If the temperature **drops too much**, the scrotal muscles **contract** and pull the testes **close to the body** to warm them. Even **tight underwear** that warms the testes can lower fertility.

**Penis:** made of **spongy (erectile) tissue and muscle**. During sexual arousal the spaces in the spongy tissue **fill with blood**, so the penis enlarges and hardens — an **erection** — and can enter the vagina to deposit semen.

**Foreskin and circumcision:** the tip of the penis is covered by a loose skin, the **foreskin**. Its surgical removal is **circumcision**. Hygiene point: an uncircumcised man must clean under the foreskin daily to avoid odour and bacterial infection.

cards.title: Male organs at a glance
head: Organ
Type
Main function
rows: Makes sperm (seminiferous tubules) and testosterone (Leydig cells)
Carries sperm from epididymis to urethra
Thin milky alkaline fluid that neutralises acid
Deposits semen in the vagina; carries urine

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is considered a primary male sexual characteristic?

options.C: The presence of the testes and penis

cards.why:
**Step 1: Define primary sexual characteristics**
Primary sexual characteristics refer to the anatomical structures directly involved in reproduction that are present at birth.

**Step 2: Identify from options**
Testes and the penis are reproductive organs present at birth. Deep voice, broad shoulders, and facial hair are secondary sexual characteristics that emerge during puberty.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **The presence of the testes and penis**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The scrotum maintains the temperature of the testes at which of the following ranges relative to core body temperature?

options.C: Exactly equal to core body temperature

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand testicular temperature requirements**
Viable spermatogenesis requires a temperature slightly lower than the core body temperature of $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**Step 2: Identify the scrotum function**
The scrotum is situated outside the pelvic cavity, cooling the testes by approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core body temperature.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **$$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ lower**.

cards.title: Male and female organs
head: Organ
Function
rows: Holds testes slightly cooler than body temperature

cards.title: Step by step: the male reproductive system
body: **Step 1:** Testes (in the scrotum) produce sperm and the hormone testosterone; the scrotum keeps them about **3–5 °C below** body temperature, which sperm production needs.
**Step 2:** Sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis.
**Step 3:** During ejaculation sperm travel through the vas deferens (sperm duct) to the urethra.

**Step 4:** Glands add seminal fluid: seminal vesicles (alkaline fluid, prostaglandins, sugar), prostate gland (thin milky alkaline fluid that neutralises acidity) and Cowper’s glands (lubricating mucus); sperm + fluid = semen.
**Step 5:** The urethra in the penis carries semen out of the body.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "SEVEN UP"
body: Seminiferous tubules, Epididymis, Vas deferens, Ejaculatory duct, (Nothing), Urethra, Penis.

cards.title: Memory hook — what the three glands add: “SPC”
body: Go down the urethra in order of the glands: **S**eminal vesicles → **P**rostate → **C**owper’s.

cards.title: Traps examiners love (2.2)
body: **Made vs stored:** sperm are **made** in the seminiferous tubules but **stored and matured** in the epididymis.
**Tubules vs Leydig cells:** tubules = sperm (FSH); Leydig (interstitial) cells = testosterone (LH).
**Vas deferens ≠ urethra:** the vas deferens carries only sperm; the urethra carries semen **or** urine.
**Which part enters the ovum?** The **head** (with its nucleus). The middle piece and tail are left outside.
**Prostate fluid is alkaline, not acidic** — it neutralises acid.
**Descent of the testes** is caused by **testosterone**, not by FSH.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: When asked for functions, give a reason too: e.g. "the scrotum is outside the body to keep the testes cooler, because sperm are made best below body temperature".

cards.title: Activity 2.2 Q1 — undescended testes
cards.problem: What happens if the testes fail to descend into the scrotum? Why?

steps.text: Step 1: Recall where sperm are made best — at 3–5 °C **below** body temperature.
Step 2: A testis that stays in the abdomen is kept at full body temperature (37 °C).
Step 3: At this temperature spermatogenesis fails, so few or no healthy sperm are made.
Step 4: If both testes stay inside, the man is **sterile (infertile)**, although testosterone may still be made, so he still develops male characters.
Step 5: The condition (cryptorchidism) is usually corrected by a small operation in early childhood.

cards.answer: The man becomes infertile because the higher body temperature stops sperm production; testosterone and male features may be normal.

cards.title: Activity 2.2 Q2 — adaptations of sperm
cards.problem: How are sperm cells adapted to perform their function?

steps.text: Step 1: Function = reach the ovum, enter it and deliver the father’s genes.
Step 2: Reach it → long **tail** for swimming; **mitochondria** in the middle piece supply energy.
Step 3: Enter it → **acrosome** enzymes dissolve the ovum’s outer coats.
Step 4: Deliver genes → head with a **haploid nucleus** (23 chromosomes); little cytoplasm so it is small and streamlined.
Step 5: Made in huge numbers → greater chance that one reaches the ovum.

cards.answer: Tail (swimming), mitochondria (energy), acrosome (enzymes to penetrate the ovum), haploid nucleus (genes), small streamlined shape and huge numbers.

cards.title: Exercise 2.2 Q1
cards.problem: What will happen to mature sperm cells that are not released from the body?

steps.text: Step 1: Sperm are stored in the epididymis for a limited time.
Step 2: Old sperm that are not ejaculated break down.
Step 3: Their materials are reabsorbed by the body.

cards.answer: They break down and are absorbed by the male’s body.

cards.title: Exercise 2.2 Q2
cards.problem: What is spermatogenesis?

steps.text: Step 1: “Sperm” + “genesis” (origin, making).
Step 2: Where — seminiferous tubules of the testes; when — from puberty.
Step 3: How — spermatogonia → mitosis → meiosis → spermatids → sperm.

cards.answer: Spermatogenesis is the formation of sperm cells from spermatogonia in the seminiferous tubules of the testes, beginning at puberty.

cards.title: Exercise 2.2 Q3
cards.problem: What is the function of the seminal fluid?

steps.text: Step 1: Name the source — seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper’s glands.
Step 2: Medium — gives a liquid for sperm to swim in.
Step 3: Food and enzymes — sugar for energy, enzymes that activate sperm.
Step 4: Alkaline — neutralises acid in the male urethra and the vagina.
Step 5: Prostaglandins — cause contractions in the female tract that help sperm move to the ovum; mucus lubricates.

cards.answer: It carries the sperm, feeds and activates them, neutralises acids, helps their movement in the female tract and lubricates.

cards.title: Exercise 2.2 Q4
cards.problem: Which part of the sperm cell enters the ovum and is involved in fertilization?

steps.text: Step 1: The acrosome releases enzymes that open a path through the ovum’s coats.
Step 2: The **head** with its nucleus enters the ovum.
Step 3: The sperm nucleus fuses with the ovum nucleus → zygote.

cards.answer: The head (its nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus); the acrosome helps it get in.

cards.title: Let us discuss — is one parent’s gamete enough?
cards.problem: In sexual reproduction, is the gamete produced by one parent enough to produce a zygote? Why?

steps.text: Step 1: Gametes are made by meiosis, so each has only **half** the chromosomes (23 in humans).
Step 2: A zygote must have the full **46**.
Step 3: So a sperm (23) must fuse with an ovum (23) → 46.

cards.answer: No. Each gamete is haploid (23 chromosomes); fusion of a male and a female gamete restores the diploid number (46) in the zygote.

cards.title: Apply it — vasectomy
cards.problem: A man has both vasa deferentia cut and tied. Explain whether he still (a) ejaculates, (b) is fertile, (c) has a deep voice.

steps.text: Step 1: (a) The glands are untouched, so he still ejaculates semen — but it contains **no sperm**.
Step 2: (b) With no sperm in the semen he is **infertile** (vasectomy is a permanent contraceptive).
Step 3: (c) Testosterone goes into the **blood**, not through the vas deferens, so male characters stay normal.

cards.answer: (a) Yes, semen without sperm; (b) no, he is sterile; (c) yes, testosterone still reaches the blood.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Why are the testes outside the abdominal cavity?

options.A: To make room for the bladder
options.B: Body temperature is too high for normal sperm production
options.D: So that semen can be stored

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Sperm are made best at 3–5 °C below body temperature.

**Step 2:** The scrotum holds the testes outside the warm abdomen.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which part of the sperm contains many mitochondria?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Mitochondria release energy.

**Step 2:** They are packed in the middle piece, close to the tail they power.

**Answer: C.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Sperm are stored and matured in the
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Tubules make sperm.

**Step 2:** The epididymis, on the outside of each testis, stores and matures them.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which secretion lubricates the end of the penis before intercourse?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Lubricate = slippery = mucus.

**Step 2:** Cowper’s glands secrete mucus-like fluid.

**Answer: C.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the scrotum becomes too cold, its muscles

options.A: relax and the testes hang lower
options.B: contract and pull the testes close to the body

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Too cold → testes must be warmed.

**Step 2:** Scrotal muscles contract and pull the testes towards the warm body.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The male reproductive system **does not** include
cards.why: The male reproductive system consists of the testes, scrotum, penis, and glands like the prostate and epididymis. The **vulva** is the collective term for the external female genitalia, thus it is not part of the male system.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which male accessory sex gland secretes a thin, alkaline fluid containing proteolytic enzymes that liquefy semen?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify male accessory glands**
The glands are the seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands.

**Step 2: Analyze prostate secretions**
The prostate gland secretes a slightly alkaline, milky fluid that contains enzymes to liquefy the semen clot after ejaculation.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Prostate gland**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Which male accessory sex gland secretes a thin, alkaline fluid containing proteolytic enzymes that liquefy semen?

steps.text: **Step 1: Identify male accessory glands**
The glands are the seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands.
**Step 2: Analyze prostate secretions**
The prostate gland secretes a slightly alkaline, milky fluid that contains enzymes to liquefy the semen clot after ejaculation.
**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Prostate gland**.

cards.title: 2.3 The female reproductive system — what it must do
body: **Five jobs:** make **ova** (eggs) and female sex hormones; receive sperm (**conception**); hold and feed the **developing fetus**; give **birth**; and **feed the baby** with milk.
**Internal (major) organs:** **ovaries, fallopian tubes (oviducts), uterus, vagina** — all inside the pelvis.
**External (accessory) organs:** the **vulva** and the **mammary glands** (breasts).
**Compare with the male:** ovary ↔ testis (gonad); oviduct ↔ sperm duct (tube); but the female has a uterus to carry the baby, so her system has **more jobs** than the male’s.

cards.title: The female organs — from ovary to the outside

steps.text: **Ovaries** — two oval glands; make ova and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone.
**Fallopian tubes** — funnel with fimbriae catches the ovum; cilia move it; **fertilization happens here** (upper part).
**Uterus (womb)** — muscular, pear-shaped; the embryo implants in its lining (endometrium).
**Cervix** — the muscular neck of the uterus that projects into the vagina.
**Vagina** — 10–15 cm tube; receives the penis and sperm; the birth canal.

cards.title: Ovaries — the female gonads
body: **Position:** two **oval** organs in the pelvis, **one on each side of the uterus**, attached to the body wall and anchored to the uterus by the **ovarian ligament**.
**When they start:** at **puberty** the **pituitary** (FSH and LH) stimulates them to become functional.
**Job 1 — ova.** Each ovum develops inside a fluid-filled **follicle**. About once a month one follicle bursts and releases its ovum — **ovulation**.

**Job 2 — hormones.** The **follicle** makes **oestrogen** (female characters, rebuilds the uterine lining). After ovulation the empty follicle turns into the **corpus luteum** (“yellow body”), which makes **progesterone** to prepare and keep the uterus ready for a fertilized ovum.
**So the ovary, like the testis, is a mixed gland:** gametes out, hormones into the blood.

cards.title: Oogenesis — the numbers behind the eggs
body: **Step 1 — at birth:** a girl’s ovaries already hold about **two million** potential ova. No new ones are made after birth (very different from sperm).
**Step 2 — before puberty:** about **75 %** degenerate, leaving a few **hundred thousand**.
**Step 3 — puberty to menopause:** each month **one** ovary releases **one** ovum ready for fertilization. Over a lifetime only **400–500** become mature ova.

**Step 4 — the meiosis twist (extra):** egg cells start meiosis before birth and pause; the ovum completes meiosis only if a sperm enters. Each division gives **one large ovum** (with nearly all the cytoplasm) and tiny **polar bodies** that die.
**Definitions:** **oogenesis** = production of ova in the ovaries; **ovulation** = release of a mature ovum from the ovary; **menopause** = the end of menstrual cycles.

cards.title: Structure of the ovum
body: **Nucleus** — the mother’s 23 chromosomes. **Cytoplasm with yolk** — food for the first days after fertilization. **Jelly coat** and **follicle cells** — protective layers the sperm’s acrosome enzymes must dissolve. **No tail** — the ovum is moved by cilia and muscle in the oviduct.

cards.title: Sperm vs ovum
head: Feature
Sperm
Ovum
rows: One per month; 400–500 in a lifetime
Stock fixed at birth; released puberty → menopause
A few days in the female tract

cards.title: Fallopian tubes (oviducts) — the meeting place
body: **Structure:** two tubes, one each side of the uterus. Each starts as a **funnel** with finger-like **fimbriae** lying close to (but **not joined to**) the ovary, runs downward and inward, and joins the top of the uterus.
**Catching the ovum:** at ovulation the fimbriae sweep over the ovary and the ovum is drawn into the funnel.
**Moving the ovum:** the ovum cannot swim. **Cilia** lining the tube beat towards the uterus and the muscular wall contracts gently (peristalsis).
**Fertilization site:** sperm swim up to meet the ovum in the **upper region of the fallopian tube**. The zygote then takes several days to reach the uterus.
**Why a blocked tube matters:** if the tubes are blocked (e.g. by infection) sperm and ovum cannot meet → infertility; tying the tubes (tubal ligation) is a permanent contraceptive.

cards.title: The uterus (womb) and cervix — the life-support system
body: **Shape and size:** a hollow, muscular, **pear-shaped** organ (the textbook prints “pearl-shaped” — it means pear), about the size of a **fist** when not pregnant. It lies **behind the bladder** (and in front of the rectum).

**Three layers (extra detail):** outer covering; thick **muscle (myometrium)** that contracts strongly in labour; inner lining (**endometrium**) rich in blood vessels and glands — thickens every month and is shed at menstruation.
**Function:** the place where the fertilized egg **implants, receives nourishment and develops into a fetus**. It stretches enormously during pregnancy and pushes the baby out at birth.
**Cervix:** the lower, muscular **neck** of the uterus that projects into the vagina. It stays tightly closed during pregnancy and **dilates (widens)** during childbirth.

cards.title: Vagina, vulva and mammary glands
body: **Vagina:** a muscular tube **10–15 cm** long connecting the uterus (cervix) to the outside. It **receives the penis and sperm**, lets the menstrual flow out, and is the **birth canal**. It is **separate from the urethra** (unlike the male, the female has separate openings for urine and reproduction).

**Hymen:** a thin mucous membrane partly covering the vaginal opening. It usually has **one or more holes**, which let menstrual blood out; the openings are usually enlarged at first intercourse — but the hymen can also stretch or tear in **sport, heavy exercise or accidents**, so its state is **not** proof of virginity.

**Vulva:** the **external genitalia** — the **vestibule** (space into which the vagina and urethra open) with its surrounding structures: outer lips (**labia majora**), inner lips (**labia minora**) and, in front, the small sensitive **clitoris** with erectile tissue.
**Mammary glands:** organs of **milk production** inside the breasts. They enlarge at puberty under **oestrogen and progesterone**; after birth **prolactin** makes milk and **oxytocin** ejects it.

cards.title: Female organs at a glance
head: Organ
Where / what
Main function
rows: Catches ovum; site of fertilization; carries zygote
Implantation, nourishment, growth of fetus; labour
Closes uterus in pregnancy; dilates at birth
Receives sperm; menstrual exit; birth canal

cards.title: Memory hook — the egg’s route: “Only The Ugly Cat Visits”
body: Say it as you trace the diagram from the side to the middle and down.

cards.title: Female path
body: Ovary (egg + oestrogen/progesterone) → oviduct (fertilisation address) → uterus (implants) → cervix → vagina.

cards.title: Exercise 2.3 Q1 / Activity 2.4 — the hymen
cards.problem: What is the hymen? How does the menstrual flow leave the uterus when the hymen is present? Does the absence of an intact hymen show that a woman has had intercourse?

steps.text: Step 1: Definition — a thin mucous membrane that partly covers the vaginal opening.
Step 2: It normally has **one or more openings**, so menstrual blood flows out through them.
Step 3: The hymen can stretch or tear during heavy exercise, sport, cycling, horse-riding or accidents; some girls are born with very little hymen.
Step 4: So an absent or torn hymen is **not proof** of intercourse.

cards.answer: A thin membrane over the vaginal opening with small holes through which the menstrual flow passes; it can be broken without intercourse, so its absence is not proof of sexual activity.

cards.title: Number work — how many eggs?
cards.problem: A girl is born with 2 000 000 potential ova. 75 % degenerate before puberty. How many remain at puberty, and what percentage of these will ever mature if 450 do?

steps.text: Step 2: Fraction maturing = 450 ÷ 500 000 = 0.0009.
Step 3: As a percentage = 0.0009 × 100 = **0.09 %**.

cards.title: Activity 2.5
cards.problem: (1) What is the role of the ovum in reproduction? (2) What is the function of the uterus?

steps.text: Step 1: The ovum is the female gamete — it carries the mother’s 23 chromosomes and food (yolk).
Step 2: When fertilized it forms the zygote, which grows into the new individual.
Step 3: The uterus receives the embryo, lets it implant, nourishes it through the placenta, protects it, and pushes it out at birth.

cards.answer: (1) Supplies the mother’s genes and the first food for the zygote. (2) Implantation, nourishment, protection and growth of the fetus; contractions at birth.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The corpus luteum develops from
cards.why:
**Step 1:** After the ovum leaves, the follicle remains.

**Step 2:** Under LH it becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The ovum moves along the fallopian tube by
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The ovum has no tail.

**Step 2:** Cilia lining the tube and gentle muscle contractions move it.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which structure is the birth canal?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The baby passes through the dilated cervix and then the vagina.

**Step 2:** The vagina is the corridor to the outside.

**Answer: C.**

cards.title: Cycle — 28-day story
body: FSH grows a follicle; oestrogen rebuilds the uterus lining; LH surge ~day 14 ovulates; corpus luteum makes progesterone to keep the lining; if no embryo, progesterone falls and the lining is shed (menstruation).

cards.title: Mnemonic — FOLP
body: FSH → Oestrogen → LH → Progesterone. “First Open the Lining, then Protect it.”

cards.title: Fertilisation to contraception — 30-second story
body: **Fertilisation** in the oviduct. Zygote → blastocyst implants. Placenta feeds and exchanges gases; amniotic sac cushions. Birth: oxytocin (posterior pituitary) helps contractions.
**Contraception** methods: barrier, hormonal (stop ovulation), IUD, natural / calendar (least reliable), sterilisation. Exam: name the method and the *how* (block sperm / stop egg / stop implant).

cards.title: 2.3.1 Menstruation and the menstrual cycle
body: **Step 1 — preparing a bed.** After ovulation the **corpus luteum** produces **progesterone**, which makes the uterine wall (endometrium) **thick, soft and rich in blood vessels**, ready to receive a fertilized ovum.
**Step 2 — no baby, no bed.** If the ovum is **not fertilized** or **implantation fails**, the corpus luteum dies, progesterone falls, and the thick wall **breaks down**.
**Step 3 — the flow.** The endometrial lining and the unfertilized ovum are discharged **with blood** through the vagina. This periodic flow of blood and tissue is **menstruation** (a “period”).
**Step 4 — rebuild.** After menstruation, oestrogen from a new growing follicle makes the lining **build up again**.
**The menstrual cycle** = this repeated building up and shedding of the lining plus the release of an ovum, about **every 28 days**, from **puberty** to **menopause**.

cards.title: The three phases on a 28-day timeline

steps.text: **Menstrual phase (days 1–5, 4–5 days):** blood, vessels and endometrial tissue are shed.
**Proliferative / follicular phase (days 5–14, 9–10 days):** the lining **proliferates** (grows rapidly) while ovarian follicles develop and make oestrogen.
**Ovulation (about day 14):** an LH surge makes the ripe follicle burst and release the ovum. The day varies between women and between cycles.
**Secretory / luteal phase (days 14–28, 12–14 days):** uterine glands mature and **secrete**; the **corpus luteum** (luteal) makes progesterone.

cards.title: Menstrual cycle phases
head: Phase (other name)
Days
In the ovary
In the uterus
rows: LH surge → follicle bursts, ovum released

cards.title: Why the names make sense
body: **Proliferative** = proliferation (fast growth) of the uterine mucosa. **Follicular** = the ovarian follicles develop.
**Secretory** = uterine glands secrete. **Luteal** = the corpus **luteum** is present.
**Rule:** the uterus name and the ovary name describe the **same days** from two organs.

cards.title: Menopause — when the cycles stop
body: **When:** at about **40–50 years**, cycles become **irregular**, ovulation stops, and finally cycles stop completely — **menopause**.
**Why:** age-related changes in the ovaries — **very few follicles remain**, and those that remain are **less sensitive to FSH and LH**, however high these hormones are.
**Result:** oestrogen and progesterone fall, so FSH and LH actually **rise** (no negative feedback).
**Males (Activity 2.7 Q3):** men have **no true menopause** — sperm and testosterone production fall only slowly with age.

cards.title: Calculate — ovulation and the fertile days
cards.problem: Ruth’s period started on 3 March and her cycles are a regular 28 days. (a) On what date does she probably ovulate? (b) Ovulation happens about 14 days before the NEXT period. If Selam has a regular 32-day cycle, on which cycle day does she ovulate?

steps.text: Step 1: Day 1 = 3 March, so day 14 = 3 + 13 = **16 March**.
Step 2: For a 32-day cycle, the luteal phase is still about 14 days.
Step 3: Ovulation day = 32 − 14 = **day 18**.
Step 4: Fertile window: sperm live a few days and the ovum ≈ 24 h, so the days just before and on ovulation are most fertile — this is why “safe-period” counting is unreliable when cycles vary.

cards.title: Explain — why menstruation stops in pregnancy
cards.problem: Why does a pregnant woman not menstruate?

steps.text: Step 1: Menstruation happens when progesterone falls.
Step 2: In pregnancy the corpus luteum, and later the **placenta**, keep secreting progesterone (and oestrogen).
Step 3: High progesterone keeps the lining in place and stops new follicles developing, so no ovulation or menstruation.

cards.answer: Progesterone stays high (corpus luteum, then placenta), so the lining is not shed and ovulation is prevented.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The secretory phase is also called the luteal phase because
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Luteal comes from corpus luteum.

**Step 2:** It is present from ovulation to the end of the cycle.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: 2.3.2 Hormonal control of reproduction — the chain of command
body: **Step 1 — brain.** The **hypothalamus** produces **gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)**, which travels to the anterior pituitary.
**Step 2 — pituitary.** GnRH makes the pituitary secrete **FSH** and **LH**.

**Step 3 — puberty switch.** Before puberty a small amount of testosterone and other **androgens** **inhibit** GnRH release. At puberty the hypothalamus becomes **less sensitive** to this inhibition, GnRH rises, and so do LH and FSH.
**Step 4 — FSH** stimulates the **seminiferous tubules** (sperm formation) in males and the **growth of follicles** in females; the cells round a developing ovum make **oestrogen**.
**Step 5 — LH** makes the **interstitial cells** of the testes secrete more **testosterone**; in females it causes ovulation and makes the **corpus luteum** produce **progesterone**.

**Step 6 — the outcome.** If the egg is fertilized, progesterone **keeps the uterine lining** from breaking down. If not, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone stops, and **menstruation** follows.

cards.title: Table 2.1 expanded — reproductive hormones
head: Hormone
Main source
Target
Main effect
rows: Gamete production (ovum and sperm); oestrogen production
Thickens uterine lining; female sexual characteristics
Prepares and maintains lining for implantation

cards.title: Feedback — how the hormones talk to each other
body: **Negative feedback (most of the cycle):** rising oestrogen and progesterone (or testosterone in males) **reduce** GnRH, FSH and LH. This keeps only **one** follicle developing at a time and keeps male hormone levels steady.
**Positive feedback (just before ovulation):** when oestrogen from the ripe follicle reaches a **high peak**, it does the opposite and triggers a **surge of LH** → ovulation.
**After ovulation:** high progesterone holds FSH and LH down, so no new follicle grows; when the corpus luteum dies, the brake is released and FSH rises again → a new cycle.
**Application:** the contraceptive pill supplies oestrogen/progesterone, keeping FSH and LH low, so no follicle matures and no ovulation occurs.

cards.title: Memory hook — order of hormones in a cycle: FOLP
body: “**F**irst **O**pen the **L**ining, then **P**rotect it.”

cards.title: Activity 2.6 Q1
cards.problem: What is the function of the testosterone found in males before puberty?

steps.text: Step 1: Before birth, testosterone from the developing testes makes them **descend into the scrotum** and the male organs form.
Step 2: In childhood the small amount present **inhibits GnRH**, so FSH and LH stay low.
Step 3: This keeps puberty from starting too early.

cards.answer: It causes descent of the testes (before birth) and, in childhood, inhibits GnRH release so that puberty does not start early.

cards.title: Activity 2.6 Q2
cards.problem: Can fertilization take place in the uterus? Why?

steps.text: Step 1: The ovum lives only about **24 hours** after ovulation.
Step 2: It moves slowly down the tube and needs several days to reach the uterus.
Step 3: So by the time it reaches the uterus it has degenerated; normally fertilization occurs in the **upper fallopian tube**.

cards.answer: Normally no — the ovum dies within about 24 hours, long before it reaches the uterus, so fertilization happens in the upper oviduct.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: At puberty GnRH secretion increases because the hypothalamus

options.B: becomes less sensitive to the inhibitory effect of androgens

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Before puberty androgens hold GnRH back.

**Step 2:** At puberty the hypothalamus becomes less sensitive to that brake → more GnRH.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: 2.3.3 Fertilization and pregnancy — the journey step by step
body: **Step 1 — ovulation.** Roughly every **28 days** one ovum is released, usually **alternately** from the two ovaries. Cilia move it down the fallopian tube. It lives only about **24 hours**.

**Step 2 — sperm arrive.** During intercourse (copulation) millions of sperm are released into the vagina. They swim through the cervix and uterus into the fallopian tube. (The textbook gives 3–5 million per cm³ of semen; medical references give tens of millions per cm³ — remember simply “millions”.) Sperm can live in the female tract for **a few days**.

**Step 3 — fertilization.** Several sperm reach the ovum, but **only one** enters. Its nucleus **fuses** with the ovum nucleus → **zygote** (46 chromosomes). This happens in the **upper region of the fallopian tube**.
**Step 4 — cleavage.** The zygote divides by **mitosis** — 2, 4, 8, 16 cells… — forming a ball of cells while moving down the tube. Pregnancy has begun.
**Step 5 — implantation.** The ball of cells reaches the uterus and the embryo **implants** in the thickened wall, obtaining food from it.
**Step 6 — keeping the pregnancy.** Progesterone (corpus luteum) maintains the uterus and stops follicles developing → no ovulation, no menstruation.

cards.title: Placenta, membranes and umbilical cord
body: **Placenta:** a special tissue made by the growing embryo and firmly joined to the uterine wall. It **absorbs nutrients and oxygen** from the mother and passes **wastes (CO₂, urea)** back. As it grows it secretes **oestrogen and progesterone**; then the corpus luteum degenerates and the placenta keeps the embryo attached.
**Chorion:** the outer membrane that protects the embryo (and forms part of the placenta).
**Amnion:** a sac containing **amniotic fluid** — a watery environment and a **shock absorber**.

**Umbilical cord:** a long cord joining the embryo to the placenta. The **umbilical vein** carries **food and oxygenated blood** to the embryo; the **umbilical arteries** carry **wastes and deoxygenated blood** back to the placenta. (Vessels are named by direction — veins go **towards** the heart, arteries **away** — not by how much oxygen they carry.)

**No direct mixing:** mother’s and baby’s blood do **not** mix; materials diffuse across the thin barrier **in the placenta** (the textbook says “through the umbilical cord” — the cord only carries the baby’s blood to and from the placenta).
**Gestation:** pregnancy usually lasts **38–40 weeks** (about 9 months).

cards.title: Exchange across the placenta
head: From mother to fetus
From fetus to mother
Kept apart
rows: Glucose, amino acids, fats, vitamins, minerals
Antibodies; but also alcohol, nicotine, some drugs and viruses (e.g. HIV) can cross

cards.title: Twins compared (Exercise 2.3 Q3)
head: Type
How formed
Genes and sex
Placenta / body
rows: Two ova released and each fertilized by a different sperm
Different, like ordinary siblings; may be different sexes
