cards.title: Exercise 2.3 Q3 — twins
cards.problem: What are the differences between fraternal, identical and Siamese twins?

steps.text: Step 1: Count the eggs and sperm — fraternal: **2 ova + 2 sperm**; identical and Siamese: **1 ovum + 1 sperm**.
Step 2: Genes — fraternal twins differ (may be boy and girl); identical/Siamese have the same genes and sex.
Step 3: Separation — identical twins separate fully; Siamese twins do not and are born joined.

cards.answer: Fraternal: two eggs fertilized by two sperm — genetically different. Identical: one zygote splits into two — genetically identical. Siamese: one zygote splits incompletely — identical twins born joined.

cards.title: Number work — cleavage
cards.problem: A zygote divides by mitosis every 12 hours. How many cells are there after 2 days (assume all divisions are regular)?

steps.text: Step 1: 2 days = 48 hours = 48 ÷ 12 = 4 divisions.
Step 2: Cells double each time: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16.
Step 3: Formula: 2ⁿ = 2⁴ = 16.

cards.title: Why only a short fertile period?
cards.problem: Sperm can live a few days in the female tract. Why is the period in which fertilization can occur still short?

steps.text: Step 1: The limiting cell is the ovum.
Step 2: The ovum degenerates about 24 hours after ovulation.
Step 3: So fertilization is possible only if sperm are present in the tube in the days just before or within a day after ovulation.

cards.answer: Because the ovum survives only about 24 hours after ovulation.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The umbilical vein carries

options.B: oxygenated blood and food to the embryo

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Vein = towards the baby’s heart.

**Step 2:** It carries food and oxygen from the placenta.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The function of amniotic fluid is to

options.B: act as a shock absorber and give a watery environment

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The amnion is a fluid-filled sac.

**Step 2:** The fluid cushions the embryo.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Worked: where fertilisation
cards.problem: Usual site in humans?

steps.text: Oviduct / fallopian tube.

cards.title: 2.3.4 Childbirth (parturition) — step by step
body: **Step 1 — labour begins.** Towards the end of gestation the thick muscular wall of the uterus starts **regular, powerful contractions** (labour). **Oxytocin** from the posterior pituitary strengthens them by **positive feedback** (link to 1.1.1).
**Step 2 — the waters break.** The abdominal wall contracts too; the **amnion bursts** and amniotic fluid flows out through the vagina, **lubricating the birth canal**.
**Step 3 — opening.** The **cervix and vagina dilate** (widen).
**Step 4 — birth.** The fetus, usually **head first** towards the cervix, gradually emerges through the vagina — **birth or parturition**.
**Step 5 — afterbirth.** The cord is clamped and cut. Further contractions push out the **placenta** and the remaining part of the umbilical cord — together called the **afterbirth**.
**Step 6 — the navel.** The stump of cord on the baby dries and falls off, leaving a scar — the **navel**.
**Step 7 — care.** By instinct the baby suckles; **prolactin** makes milk and **oxytocin** lets it flow. Breast milk gives nutrients and antibodies. Humans care for their young for many years.

cards.title: Exercise 2.3 Q2 — afterbirth
cards.problem: What is afterbirth?

steps.text: Step 1: After the baby is born the uterus keeps contracting.
Step 2: These contractions expel the placenta and the part of the umbilical cord left inside.

cards.answer: The placenta and the remaining umbilical cord, pushed out by contractions of the uterus and abdominal wall after the baby is born.

cards.title: Activity 2.7 Q1
cards.problem: Is it possible to know the sex of an unborn baby? How?

steps.text: Step 1: Yes — sex is fixed at fertilization (XX girl, XY boy).
Step 2: An **ultrasound** scan (from about 18–20 weeks) shows the external genitals.
Step 3: Tests of fetal cells (amniocentesis) can show the chromosomes, but are used only for medical reasons.

cards.answer: Yes, mainly by ultrasound scanning; chromosome tests of fetal cells can also show it.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which hormone increases uterine contractions during labour?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Contractions of the uterus = oxytocin.

**Step 2:** Prolactin is for milk production; progesterone actually relaxes the uterus.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Traps examiners love (2.3)
body: **Fertilization** happens in the **oviduct**; **implantation** in the **uterus**.
**Follicle → oestrogen; corpus luteum → progesterone.** Do not swap them.
**The ovum has no tail**; it is moved by cilia.
**Umbilical vein = oxygenated** (to the baby).
**Fraternal = 2 eggs; identical = 1 egg.**
**Menstruation** = shedding of the lining because progesterone falls — not because oestrogen rises.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the structural and functional relationship between the ovaries and the fallopian tubes?

options.A: The ovaries are physically fused to the fallopian tubes to prevent egg loss.
options.B: The fallopian tubes are separate but have finger-like fimbriae that sweep the ovulated egg from the ovary.
options.C: Ovaries develop inside the fallopian tubes during fetal life.
options.D: The fallopian tubes secrete estrogen to stimulate ovarian follicle development.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze female reproductive anatomy**
The ovaries and fallopian tubes are not physically continuous. The opening of the fallopian tube lies close to the ovary.

**Step 2: Understand egg capture**
The funnel-shaped end of the fallopian tube has finger-like projections (fimbriae) that capture the released oocyte and draw it into the tube.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **The fallopian tubes are separate but have finger-like fimbriae that sweep the ovulated egg from the ovary.**

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: What is the structural and functional relationship between the ovaries and the fallopian tubes?

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze female reproductive anatomy**
The ovaries and fallopian tubes are not physically continuous. The opening of the fallopian tube lies close to the ovary.
**Step 2: Understand egg capture**
The funnel-shaped end of the fallopian tube has finger-like projections (fimbriae) that capture the released oocyte and draw it into the tube.
**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **The fallopian tubes are separate but have finger-like fimbriae that sweep the ovulated egg from the ovary.**

cards.answer: The fallopian tubes are separate but have finger-like fimbriae that sweep the ovulated egg from the ovary.

cards.q: In humans, the zygote is formed in the
cards.why: Fertilization (the union of sperm and egg to form a zygote) typically occurs in the fallopian tube (oviduct). The zygote then travels to the uterus for implantation.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In the female reproductive system, fertilization normally takes place in the:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The ovary releases an egg into the oviduct.

**Step 2:** Sperm swim up through the uterus into the oviduct, where they meet the egg.

**Step 3:** The zygote then moves to the uterus and implants in its lining.

**Tip:** Implantation happens in the uterus, fertilization in the oviduct – do not confuse them.

cards.title: 2.4 Contraception
body: Contraception can be defined as any means used to prevent a pregnancy.
Birth control includes the use of devices, drugs or surgery.
A family may be forced to determine the number of children it would like to have for reasons such as finance, the mother’s health, etc.
Contraception is used to avoid unwanted pregnancies in young girls who are not ready to take care of children.

cards.title: Step by step: Contraception
body: **Step 1:** Contraception means methods used to prevent pregnancy by stopping sperm from meeting the egg or stopping implantation.
**Step 2:** Natural methods: abstinence (100 % effective) and the rhythm/calendar method (avoiding intercourse around ovulation – unreliable).
**Step 3:** Barrier methods: male and female condoms and the diaphragm stop sperm reaching the egg; condoms also protect against STIs including HIV.
**Step 4:** Hormonal methods: the pill, injections and implants contain hormones that stop ovulation; the IUD prevents implantation.
**Step 5:** Surgical (permanent) methods: vasectomy (cutting the sperm ducts) and tubal ligation (cutting/tying the oviducts).

**Example:** A couple wants to delay children and also avoid any risk of infection: the condom is the best single choice because it is a barrier to sperm and to infections; the pill alone would not protect against STIs.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "No sex, Natural, Barrier, Hormone, Surgery"
body: the five groups of contraception, from abstinence to permanent.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: For each method state HOW it works (stops sperm, stops ovulation, stops implantation) and whether it protects against STIs.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which hormone experiences a massive surge around day 14 of the menstrual cycle, directly triggering ovulation?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review hormonal feedback leading to ovulation**
Rising estrogen levels from growing follicles trigger positive feedback, causing a rapid release of anterior pituitary hormones.

**Step 2: Identify the specific ovulation trigger**
The surge in Luteinizing Hormone ($$LH$$) is the direct trigger that causes the dominant follicle to rupture and release the egg.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Luteinizing Hormone ($$LH$$)**.

**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which contraceptive method also protects against sexually transmitted infections such as HIV?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Most methods only prevent pregnancy.

**Step 2:** A condom is a physical barrier that stops semen and body fluids passing between partners.

**Step 3:** So it reduces the risk of STIs as well as pregnancy.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which contraceptive method also protects against sexually transmitted infections such as HIV?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Only barrier methods stop body fluids from passing between partners.

**Step 2:** The pill, IUD and vasectomy prevent pregnancy but give no protection against infections.

**Step 3:** Answer: the condom.

**Tip:** Abstinence is the only 100 % effective way to prevent both pregnancy and STIs.

tips.text: Reproduction is the only means by which the continuity of life is maintained. There are two different types of reproduction: asexual and sexual.
In asexual reproduction, only one parent is required to generate offspring and no gametes or sex cells are involved.
Alternately, in sexual reproduction two individuals of the opposite sex parents are involved.
The parents produce gametes or sex cells.
The primary sexual characters are the genital organs, while secondary sexual characteristics are those anatomical and behavioural changes that take place during puberty or adolescence.
In sexual reproduction, is the gamete produced from one parent adequate enough to produce a zygote?
The male reproductive system consists of the testes, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra, seminal vesicles, Cowper’s gland, prostate gland, scrotum, and penis.
Testes: Testes, also called testicles, are the primary sex organs (gonads) of the male reproductive system.
The two testes are positioned outside the body cavity, one at either side of the penis. They are located outside the body because the body temperature is too high for normal sperm production.

The testes are ovoid structures about five centimetres in length and three centimetres in diameter. Each testis is suspended by a spermatic cord and is contained within the cavity of the sac-like scrotum.

Female path: Ovary (egg + oestrogen/progesterone) → oviduct (fertilisation address) → uterus (implants) → cervix → vagina.
Draw the sperm route as five boxes (testis → epididymis → vas deferens → [glands] → urethra) before answering any male-system question.

questions.q: A health educator at the hospital in Keren traces the route followed by sperm from the site of their formation to the point where they leave the male body through the urethra. According to the unit's SEVEN UP pathway, how many structures does a spermatozoon pass through during this journey, and what are they in order?

options.A: 4 structures: seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, urethra
options.B: 5 structures: seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, penis
options.C: 5 structures: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra, penis
options.D: 6 structures: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis

why: **Recall the SEVEN UP acronym.** The memory aid SEVEN UP gives the path of sperm: S = Seminiferous tubules, E = Epididymis, V = Vas deferens, E = Ejaculatory duct, N = Nothing (a placeholder, not a structure), U = Urethra, P = Penis. Only the six lettered structures carry sperm; the N entry is a memory aid with no anatomical counterpart.

**Check each structure against its stated role.** Seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis; the epididymis stores spermatozoa and allows them to acquire motility; the vas deferens is the thick-walled muscular duct that exits the scrotum and loops over the urinary bladder; the ejaculatory duct is where the vas deferens joins; the urethra is the final tube; and the penis delivers semen.

**Reject the distractor pathways.** Options A and B place the vas deferens before the epididymis, but sperm enter the epididymis directly from the tubules and only later are propelled into the vas deferens. Options B and C omit the ejaculatory duct, which the unit explicitly lists between the vas deferens and the urethra. Options A and C also stop at the urethra and drop the penis.
**Count and conclude.** Six lettered structures remain once the placeholder N is excluded, giving the order seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis.

**Move to the next structure.** During sexual arousal, mature sperm are propelled from the tail of the epididymis into the vas deferens, the thick-walled muscular duct that exits the scrotum, traverses the inguinal canal into the abdominal cavity, and loops over the urinary bladder.
**Identify the end point.** The vas deferens loops over the urinary bladder to join the ejaculatory duct, which is the stated end of this stretch.

questions.q: A clinical technician in Asmara records a man's core body temperature as $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. The unit states that spermatogenesis cannot occur effectively at core body temperature, and that the scrotum maintains an optimal microenvironment approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ cooler than core body temperature. Calculate the full optimal scrotal temperature range, then state which of the following scrotal measurements would fall inside that range: $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, $$34.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, $$35.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ or $$36.2^{\circ}\text{C}$$.
questions.answer: Optimal scrotal range = $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$; the only measurement inside this range is $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$.
why: **State the governing principle.** The scrotum holds the testes outside the pelvic cavity so that sperm production occurs several degrees below core temperature, because high temperatures degrade the key germinal enzymes needed for spermatogenesis. The permitted differential is $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature.
**Compute the upper end of the range.** The upper end is only $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 3^{\circ}\text{C} = 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**Compute the lower end of the range.** The lower end is $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. The optimal range is therefore $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ inclusive.

**Test each candidate measurement.** Compare each value with the interval $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C} \leq T \leq 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. For $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ the difference from core is $$4.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, which lies between $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ and $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so it is inside. For $$34.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ the difference is only $$2.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$; for $$35.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ it is $$1.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$; and for $$36.2^{\circ}\text{C}$$ it is $$0.8^{\circ}\text{C}$$. All three are less than $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature and therefore lie above $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, outside the range.
**Conclude.** The optimal scrotal temperature range is $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, and of the four measurements only $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ falls within it.

questions.q: At a clinic in Massawa the ambient heat is high, and a technician notes that a man's testes are held at the extreme cool end of the permitted range while his core temperature reads $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. If the permitted differential is $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, calculate the temperature of the testes and state how many degrees cooler than core temperature this is.
questions.answer: Testicular temperature = $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, which is $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature
why: **Identify the relevant end of the range.** The extreme cool end corresponds to the largest permitted differential, which the unit gives as $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core body temperature. Under warm conditions the dartos and cremaster muscles relax to promote heat loss, which drives the testes toward this cool end.

**Substitute the core temperature.** Using core body temperature $$= 37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, the extreme cool testicular temperature is $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**Check against the full range.** The full range spans $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 3^{\circ}\text{C} = 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, and $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ is indeed the lowest value in that interval.

**State the cooling differential.** Subtracting the testicular temperature from the core temperature gives $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 32.0^{\circ}\text{C} = 5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so the testes are held $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature.

questions.q: A man in Asmara takes a prolonged hot bath and his scrotal temperature rises to $$36.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ while his core temperature remains $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. Calculate how far this scrotal temperature lies below core temperature, and state whether it satisfies the $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential required for effective spermatogenesis.

why: **Calculate the actual differential.** The differential is core temperature minus scrotal temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 36.0^{\circ}\text{C} = 1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**Compare with the required differential.** Effective spermatogenesis requires the testes to be approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ cooler than core temperature. The measured differential of $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ is smaller than the minimum of $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so it falls short of the requirement.

**Relate the shortfall to enzyme function.** Spermatogenesis cannot proceed effectively at temperatures close to core body temperature because heat degrades key germinal enzymes. A differential of only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ leaves the testes far too warm for normal germ-cell development.

**Conclude.** The hot bath leaves the testes only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, which fails the required $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential, so sperm production is impaired.

questions.q: At a reproductive health session in Keren, a facilitator explains that the seminal vesicles contribute approximately $$60\%$$ of the total semen volume and the prostate gland about $$30\%$$, with the remainder coming from the bulbourethral glands and the spermatozoa themselves. If a single ejaculation has a total volume of $$3.0\text{ mL}$$, calculate the volume contributed by the seminal vesicles, the volume contributed by the prostate gland, and the combined volume contributed by all remaining sources.
questions.answer: Seminal vesicles $$= 1.8\text{ mL}$$; prostate gland $$= 0.9\text{ mL}$$; all remaining sources $$= 0.3\text{ mL}$$ (together these sum to the $$3.0\text{ mL}$$ total).
why: **Identify the known quantities.** Total semen volume $$= 3.0\text{ mL}$$. Seminal vesicle contribution $$= 60\%$$ of total. Prostate gland contribution $$= 30\%$$ of total. The bulbourethral glands and spermatozoa account for whatever remains.

**Calculate the seminal vesicle volume.** Multiply the total volume by the seminal vesicle fraction: $$0.60 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 1.8\text{ mL}$$. This alkaline fluid supplies fructose as metabolic fuel for sperm and prostaglandins that trigger contractions in the female reproductive tract, which is consistent with this gland providing the bulk of semen volume.

**Calculate the prostate gland volume.** Multiply the total volume by the prostate fraction: $$0.30 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 0.9\text{ mL}$$. This thin, milky, slightly alkaline fluid contains citric acid and proteolytic enzymes that liquefy the semen coagulum after ejaculation.

**Calculate the remaining volume.** First find the remaining percentage: $$100\% - 60\% - 30\% = 10\%$$. Then apply it: $$0.10 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 0.3\text{ mL}$$. This residue corresponds to the clear, viscous, pre-ejaculatory mucus of the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands together with the spermatozoa.
**Check the total.** Add the parts: $$1.8\text{ mL} + 0.9\text{ mL} + 0.3\text{ mL} = 3.0\text{ mL}$$, which matches the stated total volume, so the calculation is consistent.

**Compute the remaining share.** $$0.10 \times 2.5\text{ mL} = 0.25\text{ mL}$$, representing the clear lubricating mucus of the bulbourethral glands plus the spermatozoa.
**Verify the total.** $$1.5\text{ mL} + 0.75\text{ mL} + 0.25\text{ mL} = 2.5\text{ mL}$$, matching the sample volume.

questions.q: A man in Massawa has been unable to conceive with his partner for two years. Semen analysis shows that sperm are being produced in normal numbers but almost all of them are immotile and none has acquired fertilizing capability, while the man's reproductive hormone levels are normal. Using only the structures and functions described in this unit, identify the single structure whose function is most likely impaired, and justify your answer with two functions of that structure.
questions.answer: The epididymis. It normally stores spermatozoa and provides the biochemical maturation by which sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability; normal sperm numbers with immotile, non-fertilizing sperm point to failure of exactly these two functions.
why: **Note that sperm production itself is intact.** The seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis and the Sertoli cells provide nutrients and structural support to developing germ cells. Because sperm are produced in normal numbers, this function is clearly not the problem. The acrosome, which carries the hydrolytic enzymes needed to digest the egg's protective layers, is also formed during spermiogenesis in the testis, so the production line is working.

**Identify which function is missing.** The two missing features are motility and fertilizing capability. The unit states that sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability during their residence in the epididymis, where they undergo biochemical maturation over several weeks.

**Match the missing functions to the correct structure.** The epididymis is the crescent-shaped tubule coiled on the superior-posterior margin of each testis in which spermatozoa reside for several weeks. Its two functions are (i) storing spermatozoa and (ii) facilitating the biochemical maturation by which sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability. An impairment of this structure explains normal sperm numbers with immotile, non-fertilizing sperm.

**Confirm that the other ducts are not implicated.** The vas deferens is a thick-walled muscular duct that simply transports mature sperm from the tail of the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct; it does not mature sperm. The unit also notes that mature sperm are propelled from the tail of the epididymis into the vas deferens only during sexual arousal, whereas the immotility described here is a property of the sperm themselves, present regardless of arousal.

**Conclude.** The impaired structure is the epididymis, because the sperm have normal production but lack precisely the two properties, motility and fertilizing capability, that the epididymis confers during maturation.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man in Asmara undergoes a vasectomy in which the vas deferens is cut and sealed. His testes continue to produce sperm and his Leydig cells continue to secrete testosterone. Explain, using only the unit's description of the male tract and of semen composition, what happens to the sperm produced after the operation and why the operation does not reduce his testosterone levels.
questions.answer: Sperm are still produced in the seminiferous tubules and mature in the epididymis, but they can no longer pass beyond the sealed vas deferens, so they are not included in the ejaculate; testosterone is unaffected because it is secreted by the Leydig cells, which the unit places under the control of LH from the anterior pituitary, not under the control of the vas deferens.
why: **Locate the cut in the pathway.** The vas deferens is the thick-walled muscular duct that carries mature sperm from the tail of the epididymis out of the scrotum, through the inguinal canal and over the urinary bladder to the ejaculatory duct. Sealing it blocks this single transport route.

**Trace the fate of the sperm.** Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules is unaffected, and sperm still pass into the epididymis to mature. However, they cannot be propelled beyond the blocked vas deferens, so no sperm reach the ejaculatory duct and urethra and none appear in the ejaculate, which is why vasectomy is a permanent surgical contraceptive method.

**Locate the source of testosterone.** In the interstitial space between adjacent seminiferous tubules lie the Leydig cells, which synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone from the anterior pituitary. These cells are entirely separate from the vas deferens.

**Explain why testosterone is unchanged.** Because the Leydig cells and the HPG axis that regulates them are untouched by the operation, testosterone secretion continues normally. Only the sperm delivery route, not the endocrine function of the testis, has been interrupted.

**Conclude.** After vasectomy, sperm are produced and matured but can no longer leave the tract, while testosterone levels remain normal because Leydig cells under LH control continue to secrete androgen independently of the vas deferens.

questions.q: A student in Keren claims that because the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands release a clear fluid before ejaculation, that fluid must be the main carrier of sperm. Explain, using the unit's description of the male accessory glands, why this claim is incorrect, and state the two functions the bulbourethral glands actually perform.
questions.answer: The claim is incorrect because the bulbourethral glands contribute only a small clear, viscous pre-ejaculatory mucus; the bulk of semen volume comes from the seminal vesicles (about 60%) and the prostate gland (about 30%). Their two functions are lubricating the urethra and neutralizing residual acidic urine prior to ejaculation.
why: **Establish the actual volume contributions.** The unit states that the seminal vesicles contribute approximately $$60\%$$ of total semen volume and the prostate gland about $$30\%$$. Together these two glands account for about $$90\%$$ of semen, leaving only roughly $$10\%$$ for the bulbourethral gland secretion and the spermatozoa themselves.

**Show why the student's claim fails.** A secretion that forms only a small fraction of the ejaculate cannot be its main carrier of sperm. The spermatozoa themselves are the cellular component, suspended in the fluid vehicle formed mainly by the seminal vesicles and prostate gland.

**State the real functions of the bulbourethral glands.** The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands secrete a clear, viscous, pre-ejaculatory mucus whose functions are to lubricate the urethra and to neutralize residual acidic urine before semen passes. These are preparatory and protective roles, not a sperm-carrying role.

**Conclude.** The claim is incorrect: the bulbourethral secretion is a minor pre-ejaculatory lubricating and neutralizing fluid, while the seminal vesicles and prostate gland provide the bulk of the semen volume.

questions.q: A man's blood testosterone level rises well above its normal stable value. Applying the negative feedback loop described in this unit, which of the following correctly states the resulting changes?

options.A: Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to increase GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to increase LH release, so testosterone production rises further.
options.B: Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release, so Leydig cell stimulation falls and testosterone production is reduced.
options.C: Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion but on the anterior pituitary to increase LH release, so the two effects cancel and testosterone production is unchanged.
options.D: Testosterone acts directly on the seminiferous tubules to decrease spermatogenesis, and the reduced sperm numbers feed back on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release.

why: **Identify the axis being regulated.** Testosterone secretion is governed by the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) axis: the hypothalamus releases Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH), which drives the anterior pituitary to release LH, and LH stimulates the Leydig cells of the testis to synthesize and secrete testosterone.

**State the direction of a negative feedback loop.** In negative feedback, a rise in the level of the final hormone in the chain suppresses the earlier steps of the chain. The unit states explicitly that as blood testosterone levels rise, testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release, stabilizing hormone levels.

**Evaluate each option.** Option A describes positive feedback, in which rising testosterone would further increase GnRH and LH, which contradicts the stabilizing negative feedback the unit describes; it also misstates the effect on both organs. Option C is internally inconsistent, since the unit gives decreases at both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary. Option D introduces a sperm-count feedback signal that the unit never describes, and the unit's loop is defined by blood testosterone acting on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, not on the seminiferous tubules.

**Confirm the correct option and its consequence.** Option B matches the unit exactly: decreased GnRH and decreased LH. With less LH reaching the Leydig cells, the interstitial cells are less stimulated, testosterone secretion falls, and the elevated blood level is brought back down toward its stable value.
**Conclude.** Rising blood testosterone suppresses the HPG axis at both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, so option B is the correct statement of the feedback response.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A laboratory report for a patient in Asmara shows a very low blood testosterone level together with an abnormally high LH level, and the hypothalamic GnRH secretion is found to be high. Which single structure does this pattern indicate is failing, and what is the normal response of that structure to LH?
questions.answer: The Leydig cells (interstitial cells) of the testis are failing. Normally LH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, so unrepaired Leydig cells should raise testosterone output when LH is high.
why: **Read the pattern of hormones.** GnRH is high and LH is high, so the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary are both sending strong stimulatory signals down the HPG axis. The defect therefore lies below the pituitary.

**Identify the target of LH.** The unit states that the Leydig cells, the interstitial cells lying between adjacent seminiferous tubules, synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone secreted from the anterior pituitary.

**Explain why high LH with low testosterone is diagnostic.** If the Leydig cells were responding normally, a high LH level would drive testosterone production upward. Instead testosterone remains very low, so the Leydig cells are not responding to LH stimulation and are the failing structure.

**Account for the high upstream hormones.** Because testosterone is the signal that suppresses the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, low testosterone removes that inhibition. GnRH and LH therefore remain high, which is exactly what the report shows.
**Conclude.** The failing structure is the Leydig cell population of the testis, whose normal response to LH is to synthesize and secrete testosterone.

questions.q: A man in Keren receives a treatment that keeps his blood testosterone concentration artificially high for several weeks. Predict the effect of this treatment on the secretion of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone and Luteinizing Hormone, and explain how the treatment will affect the activity of his Leydig cells.
questions.answer: GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus and LH release from the anterior pituitary will both decrease through negative feedback; with less LH stimulation the Leydig cells will become less active and their own testosterone secretion will fall.
why: **Recognise the feedback signal.** Blood testosterone is the final hormone of the HPG axis and acts as the inhibitory signal on the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary. An artificially raised level therefore acts as a strong inhibitory signal.
**Predict the hypothalamic response.** The hypothalamus responds by decreasing its secretion of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone, the hormone that normally drives the anterior pituitary.
**Predict the pituitary response.** The anterior pituitary responds to the raised testosterone directly, as well as to the reduced GnRH, by decreasing its release of Luteinizing Hormone.

**Trace the effect on Leydig cells.** Leydig cells synthesize and secrete testosterone when stimulated by LH. With LH release suppressed, the Leydig cells receive less stimulation and become less active, so the testis's own contribution to blood testosterone declines even while the external treatment maintains a high total level.
**Conclude.** Sustained high blood testosterone suppresses GnRH and LH through negative feedback, and the reduced LH stimulation in turn lowers the secretory activity of the Leydig cells.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: The site of sperm production is the
why: Step 1: sperm are made inside the testis.
Step 2: the cells lining the seminiferous tubules divide to form sperm.
Step 3: the epididymis only stores and matures them.
questions.tip: Made → tubules; stored → epididymis.

similar.q: Where is testosterone made?
similar.a: In the interstitial (Leydig) cells between the tubules.

why: Step 1: acro = tip, some = body.
Step 2: its enzymes dissolve the coats of the ovum.

questions.q: Urine and semen pass through the urethra at the same time.
why: Step 1: the urethra is a common tube for both.
Step 2: during ejaculation a muscle closes the bladder neck.
Step 3: so they never pass together → false.
questions.tip: Shared tube, different times.

similar.q: True or false: the vas deferens carries urine.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — male reproductive system

questions.q: State two reasons why the testes are found in the scrotum.
questions.answer: Sperm production needs a temperature 3–5 °C below body temperature, which the scrotum provides; the scrotal muscles can also adjust the testes’ position (and so temperature) — relaxing to cool them and contracting to warm them.
why: Step 1: temperature requirement.
Step 2: regulation by the scrotal muscles.
questions.tip: Always link scrotum → temperature → sperm.

similar.q: What may tight underwear do to fertility? Why?
similar.a: Reduce it, by holding the testes against the warm body.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — male reproductive system

questions.q: Which hormone causes the testes to descend into the scrotum?
why: Step 1: the developing testes secrete testosterone.
Step 2: testosterone stimulates their descent (textbook p.28).
questions.tip: The testes move themselves using their own hormone.

similar.q: What is the condition called when the testes do not descend?

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — male reproductive system

questions.q: Describe how spermatogenesis takes place.
questions.answer: It begins at puberty in the seminiferous tubules. Spermatogonia (formed in fetal life) divide by mitosis; some grow into spermatocytes, which divide by meiosis to form haploid spermatids; these develop a head with acrosome, a middle piece with mitochondria and a tail, becoming sperm, which are matured in the epididymis.
why: Step 1: where and when.
Step 2: mitosis → spermatocytes.
Step 3: meiosis → spermatids (23 chromosomes).
Step 4: shape change → sperm.
Step 5: maturation in the epididymis.
questions.tip: Use the order: gonia → cytes → tids → zoa.

similar.q: Why must meiosis happen in sperm formation?
similar.a: To halve the chromosome number so the zygote has 46, not 92.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — male reproductive system

questions.q: Semen consists of

options.B: sperm and secretions of the accessory glands

why: Step 1: sperm come from the testes.
Step 2: seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper’s glands add fluid.
Step 3: together = semen.
questions.tip: Semen = sperm + seminal fluid.

similar.q: Name two substances in semen besides sperm.
similar.a: Sugar (food), enzymes, alkaline fluid, prostaglandins, mucus.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — male reproductive system

questions.q: Circumcision is described as hygienic. Explain.
questions.answer: Circumcision removes the foreskin. Without the foreskin, secretions and dirt cannot collect under it, so there is less risk of odour and bacterial infection. An uncircumcised man must clean under the foreskin daily.
why: Step 1: define circumcision.
Step 2: what collects under the foreskin.
Step 3: consequence for infection.
questions.tip: Define first, then give the reason.

similar.q: What tissue in the penis fills with blood during an erection?

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — male reproductive system

questions.q: Prostaglandins in semen help fertilization by

options.B: stimulating muscular contractions in the female tract

why: Step 1: prostaglandins come from the seminal vesicles.
Step 2: they cause contractions in the female organs that help sperm move to the ovum.
questions.tip: Prostaglandins = “push” chemicals.

similar.q: What is the main role of Cowper’s gland mucus?

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — male reproductive system

questions.q: Arrange in order the structures through which sperm pass from where they are made to the outside.
questions.answer: Seminiferous tubules (testis) → epididymis → vas deferens → urethra (in the penis) → outside.
why: Step 1: made in the tubules.
Step 2: stored in the epididymis.
Step 3: carried by the vas deferens.
Step 4: leave through the urethra.
questions.tip: Use the mnemonic SEVEN UP.

similar.q: At which point do the seminal vesicle secretions join?
similar.a: Where the vas deferens joins the urethra (ejaculatory duct).

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — male reproductive system

questions.q: The epididymis lies on the outer surface of each testis.
why: Step 1: it is formed by the union of the seminiferous tubules.
Step 2: it lies in close contact with the external surface of each testis → true.
questions.tip: Epi = upon: “upon the testis”.

similar.q: What happens in the epididymis?
similar.a: Sperm are stored temporarily and mature.

similar.q: Which ovarian structure makes oestrogen?

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: In humans, fertilization normally takes place in the
why: Step 1: the ovum lives ≈24 h.
Step 2: it is still in the upper oviduct when sperm meet it.
questions.tip: Fertilization → tube; implantation → uterus.

similar.q: Where does the embryo implant?
similar.a: In the thickened wall (endometrium) of the uterus.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: The phase of the menstrual cycle between day 14 and day 28 is called the secretory or ____ phase.
why: Step 1: after ovulation the corpus luteum forms.
Step 2: its presence gives the name luteal.
questions.tip: Luteal ↔ corpus luteum ↔ progesterone.

similar.q: What is the other name of the proliferative phase?

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: A woman produces new ova throughout her life.
why: Step 1: about 2 million potential ova exist at birth.
Step 2: no new ones are made; the stock only falls → false.
questions.tip: Eggs: fixed stock at birth. Sperm: made daily.

similar.q: How many ova mature in a lifetime?

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: Menopause is mainly caused by
why: Step 1: few follicles remain at 40–50 years.
Step 2: remaining follicles respond poorly to FSH and LH.
Step 3: so ovulation and cycles stop.
questions.tip: Menopause starts in the ovary, not the pituitary.

similar.q: Are FSH levels high or low after menopause?
similar.a: High — little oestrogen to give negative feedback.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: Describe the roles of FSH and LH in the female.
questions.answer: FSH stimulates the growth of follicles in the ovary and the production of oestrogen by follicle cells. LH (its mid-cycle surge) causes ovulation and makes the corpus luteum secrete progesterone.
why: Step 1: FSH → follicle + oestrogen.
Step 2: LH → ovulation.
Step 3: LH → corpus luteum → progesterone.
questions.tip: F = Follicle; L = Luteum.

similar.q: Give the roles of FSH and LH in males.
similar.a: FSH: sperm formation in the tubules; LH: testosterone from interstitial cells.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: Identical twins are formed when

options.A: two ova are fertilized by two sperm
options.B: one zygote divides into two separate embryos
options.C: one ovum is fertilized by two sperm
options.D: a zygote divides but fails to separate

why: Step 1: identical = same genes = one zygote.
Step 2: the zygote splits into two embryos that separate fully.
Step 3: option D describes Siamese twins.
questions.tip: One egg → identical; two eggs → fraternal.

similar.q: Can fraternal twins be a boy and a girl?
similar.a: Yes — they come from two different eggs and sperm.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: Explain why menstruation stops during pregnancy.
questions.answer: The corpus luteum and then the placenta keep secreting progesterone (and oestrogen). Progesterone maintains the uterine lining and stops new follicles developing, so there is no ovulation and the lining is not shed.
why: Step 1: menstruation needs progesterone to fall.
Step 2: in pregnancy progesterone stays high.
Step 3: lining kept; ovulation stopped.
questions.tip: Link the event to the hormone level.

similar.q: Which organ takes over hormone secretion from the corpus luteum?

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: Which of the following passes from the fetus to the mother across the placenta?
why: Step 1: food and oxygen go mother → fetus.
Step 2: wastes (CO₂, urea) go fetus → mother.
questions.tip: Good things in, wastes out.

similar.q: Name one harmful substance that can cross the placenta.
similar.a: Alcohol, nicotine, some drugs, or viruses such as HIV.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: The membrane containing fluid that cushions the embryo is the ____.
why: Step 1: the amnion is the sac.
Step 2: its amniotic fluid acts as a shock absorber.
questions.tip: Amnion → amniotic fluid.

similar.q: Which membrane forms part of the placenta?

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: Describe the main events of childbirth.
questions.answer: Regular powerful contractions of the uterus begin (labour), strengthened by oxytocin; the amnion bursts and the fluid lubricates the birth canal; the cervix and vagina dilate; the baby is pushed out head first; the cord is cut; the placenta and remaining cord are expelled as the afterbirth; the cord stump falls off, leaving the navel.
why: Step 1: labour contractions.
Step 2: waters break.
Step 3: dilation.
Step 4: delivery head first.
Step 5: afterbirth.
Step 6: navel forms.
questions.tip: Write the events in time order with one key word each.

similar.q: What is the navel?
similar.a: The scar left where the umbilical cord stump fell off.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: If a woman’s cycle is 28 days and day 1 is the first day of bleeding, ovulation is most likely on
why: Step 1: menstrual phase days 1–5.
Step 2: proliferative phase to day 14.
Step 3: ovulation ≈ day 14.
questions.tip: Ovulation ≈ 14 days BEFORE the next period.

similar.q: For a 30-day cycle, about which day is ovulation?

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: State the function of each: (a) fimbriae (b) cervix (c) endometrium.
questions.answer: (a) Fimbriae sweep the released ovum into the fallopian tube. (b) The cervix closes the uterus during pregnancy and dilates during birth. (c) The endometrium thickens to receive and nourish the embryo; it is shed in menstruation.
why: Step 1: fimbriae → catch.
Step 2: cervix → close/open.
Step 3: endometrium → bed for the embryo.
questions.tip: One verb per structure: catch, close, cushion.

similar.q: What is the function of cilia in the oviduct?
similar.a: To move the ovum (or zygote) towards the uterus.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: In the female, the urethra and vagina open separately into the vestibule.
why: Step 1: the vestibule is the space into which both open.
Step 2: they are separate tubes → true.
questions.tip: Female: separate openings; male: shared urethra.

similar.q: What are the labia majora?
similar.a: The outer lips of the vulva.

units.title: The Skeletal System
units.intro: Bone is living: hard matrix (calcium salts) + collagen + cells. Compact bone outside, spongy inside, marrow in the middle (blood cells). Cartilage cushions; ligaments bone-to-bone.

f2.title: Axial = skull + spine + ribs. Appendicular = girdles + limbs.

cards.title: Axial = skull + spine + ribs. Appendicular = girdles + limbs.
3.1.1 Structure and Composition of Bone
body: A bone begins as cartilage before it is converted to bone through a process called ossification.
The key players in bone development are cartilage cells and mature bone cells.
Cut the bones into cross-sectional and longitudinal halves. c.
Examine the internal structure of the bones.

cards.title: 3.1.2 Cartilage and Ligaments
body: **Cartilage** is a type of connective tissue consisting of a tough, flexible matrix made of collagen, protein, and sugar.
Although not as hard as a bone, cartilage forms an important structural component of many parts of the skeletal system.
Much of the fetal skeleton is formed entirely of cartilage.
Cartilage exists in several forms, from glassy to fibrous in appearance.

cards.title: 3.1.3 Axial and appendicular skeletons — the two halves of the body’s frame
body: **Step 1 — the big split.** The human skeleton (about **206 bones** in an adult) is divided into two parts: the **axial skeleton** (80 bones) and the **appendicular skeleton** (126 bones).

**Step 2 — axial = the axis.** Picture a line down the middle of your body. The bones **on that central axis** form the axial skeleton: **skull, vertebral column (backbone) and thorax (sternum + ribs)**.

**Step 3 — appendicular = the appendages.** Bones **hanging from** (appended to) that axis — the **limbs (arms and legs)** and the **girdles** that join them to the axis — form the appendicular skeleton.

**Step 4 — the jobs differ.** Axial: mainly **protection** of vital organs (brain, spinal cord, heart, lungs) and a **central framework**. Appendicular: mainly **movement** and handling objects; the girdles give the limbs their wide range of movement.
**Step 5 — where they meet.** The two parts join at the **shoulders** (pectoral girdle ↔ sternum) and the **hips** (pelvic girdle ↔ sacrum).

steps.text: **Axial skeleton = 80 bones:** skull 22, ear ossicles 6, hyoid 1, vertebral column 26, sternum 1, ribs 24.
**Appendicular skeleton = 126 bones:** pectoral girdle 4, arms 60, pelvic girdle 2, legs 60.
The textbook counts 8 cranial + 14 facial bones + 3 tiny bones in each ear. The **hyoid** (a U-shaped bone in the neck that holds the tongue) completes the 80.

cards.title: A. The axial skeleton — skull
body: **Cranium (8 bones):** a strong bony box that **protects the brain**. It has small holes (perforations) through which **blood vessels and nerves** pass to and from the brain.

**Facial bones (14):** include the **upper jaw (maxilla)** and the **lower jaw (mandible)** — the only skull bone that moves (for chewing and speaking). The skull also protects the **olfactory organs (nose), the middle and inner ear and the eyes** (eye sockets).
**Ear ossicles (3 in each ear):** malleus, incus, stapes — the smallest bones in the body; they pass sound vibrations to the inner ear.

**Sutures and fontanels:** the skull bones are tightly fitted together by immovable joints (sutures). At birth many are not yet joined, leaving **“soft spots” (fontanels)** that let the skull squeeze slightly during birth and let the brain grow. They close by about **two years** of age.

cards.title: The vertebral column (backbone)
body: **Length and number:** about **70 cm** long in an adult. It is made of **33 vertebrae** in a child; in the adult the lower ones fuse, so there are **26 separate bones** (24 vertebrae + sacrum + coccyx).
**Discs of cartilage** lie between the vertebrae. They **absorb shock, reduce friction** and let the column **bend** a little at each joint — together this gives a flexible backbone.

**Three jobs:** (1) the **main support** from which the rest of the upper body branches; (2) **protects the spinal cord** (and spinal nerves) inside the vertebral canal; (3) gives **attachment** for ribs and back muscles.

**Atlas and axis:** the first two cervical vertebrae are special. The **atlas (C1)** carries the skull and allows **nodding** (“yes”); the **axis (C2)** has a peg on which the atlas turns, allowing **rotation** (“no”).
**Caudal vertebrae** vary between animals with the size of the tail. In humans the tail is **vestigial**, so the four caudal vertebrae fuse to form the **coccyx**.

cards.title: The five regions of the vertebral column

steps.text: **Cervical — 7** (neck). Atlas and axis move the head.
**Thoracic — 12** (chest). Each carries a pair of ribs.
**Lumbar — 5** (lower back). Largest and strongest, carry most body weight.
**Sacral — 5 fused → sacrum.** Joins the pelvic girdle.
**Caudal (coccygeal) — 4 fused → coccyx.** Remnant of a tail.

cards.title: Memory hook — vertebrae per region: “breakfast at 7, lunch at 12, dinner at 5”
body: Cervical 7 → Thoracic 12 → Lumbar 5, then Sacral 5 and Caudal 4. Say “7-12-5-5-4” like a phone number.

cards.title: The thorax — sternum and ribs
body: **Sternum (breastbone):** a flat bone about **15 cm** long in the middle of the chest.

**Ribs:** **12 pairs** (24 ribs). Every pair joins a thoracic vertebra at the back. Their main purpose is to **protect the heart and lungs**; their **cartilage** joints make the rib cage **flexible for breathing**.
**True ribs — upper 7 pairs:** joined **directly** to the sternum by their own cartilage.
**False ribs — next 3 pairs (8–10):** joined **indirectly** — their cartilage joins the cartilage of the rib above.

**Floating ribs — last 2 pairs (11–12):** **not attached to the sternum at all**; they are fixed only to the vertebrae at the back. (The textbook’s wording “the sternum is connected to all ribs except the last pair” and “attached to the last pair of ribs” is loose — remember **7 true, 3 false, 2 floating**.)

cards.title: B. The appendicular skeleton — girdles
body: **What it is:** the bones of the **appendages (limbs)** and the **girdles** that attach them to the axial skeleton.

**Pectoral (shoulder) girdle — 4 bones:** two **scapulae** (shoulder blades) and two **clavicles** (collar bones). It forms a **loose attachment** with the sternum, which lets the arms move very freely. The **scapula** rests on the back of the rib cage and gives a **broad flat surface** for arm muscles and a **socket** for the head of the humerus. The **clavicle** props the shoulder outwards and **stops it collapsing inward**.

**Pelvic (hip) girdle — 2 hip bones:** each hip bone is several bones (ilium, ischium, pubis) **fused together**; with the sacrum they form a strong **ring**. Its functions: (1) **socket** for the femur, (2) surface for **muscle attachment**, (3) **protects** lower abdominal organs (bladder, reproductive organs), (4) **transmits body weight** from the backbone to the legs.
**Why the difference?** The shoulder girdle is light and loose → **range of movement**. The hip girdle is heavy and fused → **strength and weight bearing**.

cards.title: i. The upper appendages — arm and hand (30 bones each)
body: **Upper arm — humerus (1):** the single long bone from shoulder to elbow.

**Forearm — radius and ulna (2):** the **ulna** forms the elbow joint with the humerus; the **radius** is on the **thumb side**. Two bones instead of one allow the forearm and wrist to **twist** (turn the palm up and down).
**Wrist — carpals (8):** small bones in **two irregular rows** joined by **gliding joints**, giving the wrist flexibility.
**Palm — metacarpals (5):** extend from the wrist; covered with skin they form the palm.
**Fingers — phalanges (14):** the **thumb has 2**, each other finger **3** (2 + 4×3 = 14). Phalanges are **long bones** (long in shape, though small).

**The opposable thumb:** the first metacarpal joins the wrist by a **saddle joint** while the others lie in one plane. So the thumb can swing across to touch each fingertip — letting humans **grasp objects, use tools and do skilful work**. This is one feature that makes the human skeleton unique.

cards.title: ii. The lower appendages — leg and foot (30 bones each)
body: **Thigh — femur (1):** the upper bone of the leg; the **longest, largest and strongest** bone of the body.
**Knee cap — patella (1):** a thick bone in the tendon in front of the knee; it **covers and protects** the front of the knee joint.
**Lower leg — tibia and fibula (2):** connect the femur to the ankle. The **tibia** (shin bone) is the thick, weight-bearing one; the **fibula** is thin, on the outer side.
**Ankle — tarsals (7):** include the heel bone.

**Sole — metatarsals (5).** **Toes — phalanges (14):** 2 in the big toe and 3 in each other toe — the same pattern as the hand, but **much shorter** and (in the first row) flattened sideways. (The textbook says toes are “composed of metatarsals” — the toes are phalanges; the metatarsals form the sole.)
**Foot at a right angle to the leg:** gives a broad, stable base for **standing upright and walking on two legs**.

cards.title: Arm and leg are built on the same plan
head: Part
Arm (upper limb)
Leg (lower limb)

cards.title: Memory hook — limb bones in order: “1-2-many-5-14”
body: Every limb goes **1** long bone → **2** bones → a **cluster** of small bones → **5** long bones → **14** phalanges. The leg adds the patella.

cards.title: Traps examiners love (3.1.3)
body: **Girdles belong to the appendicular skeleton**, not the axial — even though they touch the axis.
**Sternum and ribs are axial**, the clavicle and scapula are appendicular.
**Radius = thumb side; ulna = little-finger side** (forms the elbow).
**Thumb and big toe have 2 phalanges**; all other digits have 3.
**33 vs 26:** 33 vertebrae before fusion; 26 separate bones in an adult.
**Floating ribs** are free at the front — they are not joined to the sternum.

cards.title: Exercise 3.1 Q1
cards.problem: What is the appendicular skeleton? Why is it called appendicular?

steps.text: Step 1: List the bones — limbs (arms, legs) and the girdles (pectoral, pelvic).
Step 2: Explain the name — these bones are **appendages**, “hung onto” (appended to) the central axial skeleton.
Step 3: Add the number — 126 bones.

cards.answer: The appendicular skeleton is the 126 bones of the limbs and their girdles; it is called appendicular because these bones are appendages attached to the axial skeleton.

cards.title: Exercise 3.1 Q2
cards.problem: What is the advantage of the foot forming a right angle to the leg?

steps.text: Step 1: Humans stand and walk upright on two legs (bipedal).
Step 2: A foot at right angles gives a **broad flat base**, so the body is **balanced** and its weight is spread over the sole.
Step 3: The foot acts as a **lever** — the heel strikes and the toes push off — making walking and running efficient.

cards.answer: It provides a broad, stable base for upright posture and balance, spreads body weight, and acts as a lever for walking and running.

cards.title: Exercise 3.1 Q3
cards.problem: Why is the femur the longest, largest and strongest bone of the body?

steps.text: Step 1: The femur carries the **whole weight of the upper body** passed down from the pelvis.
Step 2: It must resist large forces in walking, running and jumping.
Step 3: The most **powerful muscles** of the body (thigh and buttock) attach to it, so it needs a big surface.
Step 4: Its length gives a long stride (long lever).

cards.answer: Because it bears the body’s weight transmitted from the pelvis, withstands the forces of walking and running, gives attachment to the strongest muscles and acts as a long lever.

cards.title: Exercise 3.1 Q4
cards.problem: What are the types of bones found in the human body, as classified by their shapes? Give examples.

steps.text: Step 1: Long bones — longer than wide: femur, humerus, phalanges.
Step 2: Short bones — cube-like: carpals, tarsals.
Step 3: Flat bones — thin plates that protect or anchor muscles: cranial bones, sternum, ribs, scapula.
Step 4: Irregular bones — complex shapes: vertebrae, some facial bones. (The patella is a small bone inside a tendon, often called sesamoid.)

cards.answer: Long, short, flat and irregular bones (e.g. femur; carpals; skull bones and ribs; vertebrae).

cards.title: Count it — the arm
cards.problem: Show that each upper limb has 30 bones and that both upper limbs plus the pectoral girdle make 64.

steps.text: Step 1: Humerus 1 + radius 1 + ulna 1 = 3.
Step 2: Carpals 8 + metacarpals 5 = 13 → running total 16.
Step 3: Phalanges: thumb 2 + 4 fingers × 3 = 14 → 16 + 14 = **30**.
Step 4: Two arms = 60; pectoral girdle = 2 clavicles + 2 scapulae = 4; 60 + 4 = **64**.

cards.title: Apply it — why two forearm bones?
cards.problem: A student turns a door handle and a screwdriver. Which bones make this possible and how?

steps.text: Step 1: Turning the hand palm-up/palm-down needs a twisting forearm.
Step 2: The **radius** rotates around the **ulna**, which stays fixed at the elbow.
Step 3: With a single bone this twisting would be impossible.

cards.answer: The radius rotating around the ulna allows twisting of the forearm and wrist.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which bone belongs to the axial skeleton?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Axial = skull, vertebral column, sternum, ribs.

**Step 2:** Clavicle and scapula are pectoral girdle (appendicular).

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: How many thoracic vertebrae are there?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** 7-12-5-5-4.

**Step 2:** Thoracic = 12, one for each pair of ribs.

**Answer: C.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Ribs 11 and 12 are called floating ribs because they

options.B: are not attached to the sternum

cards.why:
**Step 1:** They are joined to vertebrae at the back.

**Step 2:** At the front they are free — no link to the sternum.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The thumb can be opposed because its metacarpal joins the wrist by a
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The other metacarpals lie in one plane.

**Step 2:** The thumb’s saddle joint lets it swing across the palm.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which is a function of the pelvic girdle?

options.B: Transmits body weight from the backbone to the legs

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The pelvic girdle is a strong ring joined to the sacrum.

**Step 2:** It passes the weight of the upper body to the femurs.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following is an evolutionary advantage of an endoskeleton compared to an exoskeleton?

steps.text: **Step 1: Compare endoskeleton and exoskeleton biology**
An exoskeleton is a non-living outer casing that cannot grow.
Animals with exoskeletons must moult (shed) to grow, during which they are highly vulnerable.
**Step 2: Define endoskeleton characteristics**
An endoskeleton is composed of living tissue that grows continuously alongside the organism's body, eliminating the risky process of moulting.

cards.answer: It grows continuously with the organism, avoiding the need for periodic moulting.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: What is the name of the double-layered fibrous connective tissue membrane that covers the outer surface of a living bone?

steps.text: **Step 1: Identify bone membranes**
The endosteum lines the internal medullary cavities.
The synovial membrane lines articular joint capsules.
**Step 2: Match with outer cover**
The periosteum is the dense, fibrous double-layered membrane that covers the entire outer surface of a bone, supplying it with blood vessels, nerves, and osteoblasts.

**Step 1: Contrast marrow types**
Yellow bone marrow stores lipids (fat). Red bone marrow is rich in hematopoietic stem cells.

**Step 2: Identify physiological function**

**Step 2: State mechanical functions**
Calcium phosphate provides hardness and compression resistance. Collagen provides flexibility and tensile strength, preventing the bone from shattering easily.

**Step 3: Final Result**

The ball-and-socket joint allows movement in several directions, including rotation.
Pivot joint: Rounded or conical surfaces of one bone fit into a ring of one or more bones, allowing rotation movement.

cards.q: Which of the following is an evolutionary advantage of an endoskeleton compared to an exoskeleton?

options.A: It provides a completely sealed outer moisture barrier.
options.B: It grows continuously with the organism, avoiding the need for periodic moulting.
options.C: It does not require blood vessels or nutrients.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Compare endoskeleton and exoskeleton biology**
An exoskeleton is a non-living outer casing that cannot grow. Animals with exoskeletons must moult (shed) to grow, during which they are highly vulnerable.

**Step 2: Define endoskeleton characteristics**
An endoskeleton is composed of living tissue that grows continuously alongside the organism's body, eliminating the risky process of moulting.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **It grows continuously with the organism, avoiding the need for periodic moulting.**

**Step 2: Match with outer cover**
The periosteum is the dense, fibrous double-layered membrane that covers the entire outer surface of a bone, supplying it with blood vessels, nerves, and osteoblasts.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Periosteum**.

cards.title: Joints
body: A **joint** is where two bones meet. **Fixed (immovable):** sutures of the skull. **Slightly movable:** between vertebrae (cartilage discs). **Freely movable (synovial):** have cartilage on the bone ends and a capsule filled with **synovial fluid** that reduces friction. Examples: **ball-and-socket** (shoulder, hip: movement in all directions), **hinge** (elbow, knee: movement in one plane), **pivot** (between the first two neck vertebrae: turning the head), **gliding** (wrist and ankle bones).

cards.title: Step by step: Joints
body: **Step 1:** A joint is where two or more bones meet.
**Step 2:** Immovable (fibrous) joints: bones are fixed by fibrous tissue – sutures of the skull.
**Step 3:** Slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints: bones joined by cartilage pads – between vertebrae, pubic symphysis.
**Step 4:** Freely movable (synovial) joints: a capsule with synovial fluid (lubricant), cartilage on bone ends (reduces friction) and ligaments (join bone to bone).

**Step 5:** Types of synovial joint: ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip – movement in all directions), hinge (elbow, knee – one plane), pivot (atlas–axis, turning the head), gliding (wrist, ankle bones), saddle (thumb).
**Example:** Shoulder vs elbow: the shoulder (ball-and-socket) lets you swing the arm in a full circle; the elbow (hinge) only bends and straightens the forearm like a door.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Ball Has Pivot Glide Saddle"
body: B-H-P-G-S, the five synovial joints.

questions.q: The adult human vertebral column (spine) is made up of 33 vertebrae. Which of the following correctly matches each region of the spine with its number of vertebrae?
why: **Recall the total number of vertebrae.** The unit states that the vertebral column (spine) consists of 33 vertebrae separated by fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs, and that it is divided into five regions.
**Assign the cervical and thoracic counts.** The cervical region contains 7 vertebrae, which include the atlas and axis that permit head rotation. The thoracic region contains 12 vertebrae.

**Assign the lumbar, sacral and caudal counts.** The lumbar region contains 5 vertebrae. The sacral region contains 5 fused vertebrae that form the sacrum, and the caudal (coccygeal) region contains 4 fused vertebrae that form the coccyx.

**Check the sum and select the matching option.** Adding the regions: 7 + 12 + 5 + 5 + 4 = 33, which agrees with the stated total. Option B wrongly gives 12 cervical and 7 thoracic vertebrae; option C wrongly gives 5 thoracic, 12 lumbar, 4 sacral and 5 caudal vertebrae; option D wrongly gives only 5 cervical and 7 lumbar vertebrae. Only option A is fully consistent with the unit.

questions.q: An anatomy chart in a school laboratory in Asmara lists 8 cranial bones and 14 facial bones. Calculate the total number of bones in the skull, and state the type of joint that fuses the cranial bones together.
questions.answer: The skull contains 22 bones (8 cranial + 14 facial), and the cranial bones are fused at immovable (fibrous) joints called sutures.
why: **Identify the two groups of skull bones.** The unit divides the skull into 8 cranial bones, which are fused together to protect the brain, and 14 facial bones, which form the architecture of the face and support the teeth.
**Add the two groups.** Total skull bones = 8 cranial + 14 facial = 22 bones.
**Name the joint type.** The cranial bones are joined at immovable fibrous joints called sutures, which allow zero movement in order to protect the delicate brain tissue.

questions.q: A vertebral column model in a biology laboratory in Keren has lost 3 of its thoracic vertebrae. How many vertebrae remain in the model, and how many of the remaining vertebrae are fused?
questions.answer: 30 vertebrae remain in the model, of which 9 are fused (5 sacral and 4 caudal).
why: **State the complete column.** A complete vertebral column contains 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 4 fused caudal vertebrae.
**Subtract the lost thoracic vertebrae.** The model has lost 3 thoracic vertebrae, so the thoracic region now has 12 - 3 = 9 vertebrae and the whole column has 33 - 3 = 30 vertebrae.

**Count the fused vertebrae.** Only the sacral and caudal regions are fused: 5 sacral + 4 caudal = 9 fused vertebrae. These are unaffected by the loss of thoracic vertebrae, so 9 of the remaining 30 vertebrae are fused.

questions.q: A fresh long bone sample taken from a slaughtered ox at the abattoir in Asmara has a total mass of 480 g. In bone, the organic matrix makes up approximately $$\frac{1}{3}$$ of the total bone mass and the inorganic mineral salts make up the remaining $$\frac{2}{3}$$. (a) Calculate the mass of the organic matrix and the mass of the inorganic mineral salts in this sample. (b) The sample is then soaked in a weak acid (vinegar) for several days. State the mass of the sample that remains and describe its physical properties, giving the chemical reason for the change.
questions.answer: (a) Organic matrix = 160 g and inorganic mineral salts = 320 g. (b) 160 g of the sample remains; the bone becomes soft, flexible and rubbery because the acid dissolves the calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) mineral matrix, leaving only the organic collagen matrix.
why: **Identify the composition fractions from the unit.** The unit states that the organic portion is approximately $$\frac{1}{3}$$ of total bone mass (collagen fibres, ground substance and bone cells) and that the inorganic mineral salts are the remaining $$\frac{2}{3}$$ (mainly calcium phosphate crystals in the form of hydroxyapatite).
**Calculate the mass of the organic matrix.** Organic mass = $$\frac{1}{3} \times 480\text{ g} = 160\text{ g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of the inorganic mineral salts.** Inorganic mass = $$\frac{2}{3} \times 480\text{ g} = 320\text{ g}$$. Check: 160 g + 320 g = 480 g, which equals the total mass of the sample.

**Work out the mass remaining after the acid soak.** The weak acid dissolves the inorganic mineral matrix (the calcium phosphate salts). Only the organic collagen matrix is left intact, so the remaining mass equals the organic mass, 160 g.

**Describe the physical change and conclude.** Because the hard, rigid mineral component that gives bone its compressional strength has been removed, the bone loses its hardness and rigidity and becomes highly flexible and rubbery, so it can be bent or twisted without breaking.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A bone sample of 300 g is baked in an oven at a high temperature for several hours. Using the composition $$\frac{1}{3}$$ organic and $$\frac{2}{3}$$ inorganic, calculate the mass of the sample that remains and describe its physical properties, explaining the chemical basis for the change.
questions.answer: 200 g of the sample remains; the bone becomes extremely brittle and chalky because the heat destroys (denatures) the organic collagen matrix, leaving only the inorganic mineral salts.
why: **State the composition of the sample.** The organic matrix is $$\frac{1}{3}$$ and the inorganic mineral salts are $$\frac{2}{3}$$ of bone mass, as given in the unit.

**Calculate the mass of organic matrix destroyed.** Organic mass = $$\frac{1}{3} \times 300\text{ g} = 100\text{ g}$$. High temperature denatures the collagen fibres and proteins, so this 100 g is destroyed.
**Calculate the mass remaining.** Remaining mass = 300 g - 100 g = 200 g, which is exactly the inorganic fraction $$\frac{2}{3} \times 300\text{ g} = 200\text{ g}$$ of mineral salts.

**Describe the physical result and conclude.** With the organic matrix gone, the bone loses its flexibility and tensile strength; only the hard mineral salts remain, so the bone becomes extremely brittle, chalky and easy to shatter under minimal pressure.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A dried bone sample from a butcher's shop in Keren is found to contain 210 g of inorganic mineral salts. If the inorganic salts make up $$\frac{2}{3}$$ of bone mass, calculate the total mass of the sample and the mass of its organic matrix.
questions.answer: The total mass of the sample is 315 g and its organic matrix is 105 g.
why: **Set up the fraction relationship.** The unit states that inorganic mineral salts form $$\frac{2}{3}$$ of total bone mass. Let the total mass be $$M$$, so $$\frac{2}{3}M = 210\text{ g}$$.
**Solve for the total mass.** Multiply both sides by $$\frac{3}{2}$$: $$M = 210 \times \frac{3}{2} = 315\text{ g}$$.
**Calculate the organic mass.** Organic mass = total mass - inorganic mass = 315 g - 210 g = 105 g. Check: $$\frac{1}{3} \times 315\text{ g} = 105\text{ g}$$, which agrees.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: In a Grade 11 biology laboratory in Nakfa, students assemble a model of the adult axial skeleton, which consists of the skull, the vertebral column and the thoracic cage. Using the numbers given in the unit, (a) calculate the total number of bones in the axial skeleton by adding the skull bones (8 cranial + 14 facial), the 33 vertebrae and the thoracic cage (1 sternum + 12 pairs of ribs); and (b) express this axial total as a percentage of the 206 bones of the adult skeleton, correct to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) The axial skeleton contains 80 bones. (b) This is $$\frac{80}{206} \times 100\% \approx 38.8\%$$ of the 206 bones of the adult skeleton.
why: **Count the skull bones.** The skull = 8 cranial bones + 14 facial bones = 22 bones.
**State the number of vertebrae.** The vertebral column contains 33 vertebrae (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 4 fused caudal).
**Count the bones of the thoracic cage.** The thoracic cage = 1 sternum + 12 pairs of ribs = 1 + (12 $$\times$$ 2) = 1 + 24 = 25 bones.
**Add the three parts to obtain the axial total.** Axial skeleton = 22 + 33 + 25 = 80 bones. This agrees with the unit value of 80 bones for the axial skeleton.

**Express the axial total as a percentage of the whole skeleton.** Percentage = $$\frac{80}{206} \times 100\% = 38.8349\ldots\% \approx 38.8\%$$. Check: the appendicular skeleton is 206 - 80 = 126 bones, and $$\frac{126}{206} \times 100\% \approx 61.2\%$$, and 38.8% + 61.2% = 100%.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: The bones of one lower limb, as listed in the unit, are the femur, the patella, the tibia, the fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals and 14 phalanges. (a) Calculate the number of bones in one lower limb and in both lower limbs. (b) Express the bones of both lower limbs as a percentage of the 126 bones of the appendicular skeleton, correct to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) One lower limb has 30 bones, so both lower limbs have 60 bones. (b) $$\frac{60}{126} \times 100\% \approx 47.6\%$$ of the appendicular skeleton.
why: **List the single bones of one lower limb.** The unit lists the femur (thigh bone), the patella (kneecap), and the tibia and fibula (shin bones), which are 4 individual bones.
**Add the numbered groups of one lower limb.** One lower limb = 4 + 7 tarsals + 5 metatarsals + 14 phalanges = 4 + 7 + 5 + 14 = 30 bones.
**Calculate both lower limbs.** Both lower limbs = 2 $$\times$$ 30 = 60 bones.
**Express as a percentage of the appendicular skeleton.** Percentage = $$\frac{60}{126} \times 100\% = 47.6190\ldots\% \approx 47.6\%$$.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: The thoracic cage contains 12 pairs of ribs. The top 7 pairs are true ribs, the next 3 pairs are false ribs and the bottom 2 pairs are floating ribs. (a) Calculate the total number of individual ribs. (b) Calculate the percentage of the total ribs that are true ribs and the percentage that are floating ribs, each correct to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) There are 24 individual ribs. (b) True ribs = $$\frac{14}{24} \times 100\% \approx 58.3\%$$ and floating ribs = $$\frac{4}{24} \times 100\% \approx 16.7\%$$ of all ribs.
why: **Convert pairs of ribs into individual ribs.** 12 pairs of ribs = 12 $$\times$$ 2 = 24 individual ribs.
**Calculate the number of true ribs.** True ribs are the top 7 pairs, which connect directly to the sternum via their own costal cartilages: 7 $$\times$$ 2 = 14 ribs.
**Calculate the number of floating ribs.** Floating ribs are the bottom 2 pairs, which do not connect to the sternum at all: 2 $$\times$$ 2 = 4 ribs.

**Express each group as a percentage of 24 ribs.** True ribs: $$\frac{14}{24} \times 100\% = 58.333\ldots\% \approx 58.3\%$$. Floating ribs: $$\frac{4}{24} \times 100\% = 16.666\ldots\% \approx 16.7\%$$. The remaining 6 false ribs give $$\frac{6}{24} \times 100\% = 25.0\%$$, and 58.3% + 25.0% + 16.7% = 100%.
