questions.q: A cyclist riding from Asmara down to Massawa falls from her bicycle and injures her knee. At the hospital the doctor explains that the knee is a freely movable joint. (a) Describe the structural features of a freely movable (synovial) joint and explain how these features prevent wear and tear on the articulating bone ends during high-impact movement. (b) Classify the elbow joint, the shoulder joint and the atlas-axis joint by their mechanical shape, and state the movement that each one permits.
questions.answer: (a) In a synovial joint the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid and enclosed by an articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane. Articular (hyaline) cartilage cushions the bone ends and absorbs compressional shock, while the synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction to near zero, so wear and tear are prevented. (b) The elbow is a hinge joint (flexion and extension in a single plane), the shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint (multidirectional rotation), and the atlas-axis joint is a pivot joint (rotation around a central axis).
why: **Define the freely movable joint.** A freely movable (synovial) joint is one in which the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with lubricating synovial fluid, and the whole joint is enclosed by a tough articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane.

**Explain the role of articular cartilage.** The bone ends are covered by a layer of articular (hyaline) cartilage. This cartilage cushions the bone ends, absorbs compressional shock and minimises friction between the moving surfaces.

**Explain the role of synovial fluid and the capsule.** The synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid into the joint cavity; this slippery fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction to near zero, while the articular capsule holds the fluid in place and keeps the joint stable.
**Classify the elbow joint.** The elbow is a hinge joint, in which a convex surface fits into a concave depression, permitting flexion and extension in a single plane.

**Classify the shoulder and the atlas-axis joints.** The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, in which a ball-like head fits into a cup-like socket, allowing rotational movement in multiple planes. The atlas-axis joint is a pivot joint, in which a rounded surface rotates within a ring, allowing rotation of the head around a central axis.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A metalworker in Asmara can swing his arm freely in all directions, yet the bones of his skull cannot move at all. Compare the skull sutures and the shoulder joint in terms of the connective tissue that binds the bones, the range of movement allowed, and the protective or mechanical advantage each arrangement provides.
questions.answer: The skull sutures are immovable (fibrous) joints, bound tightly by dense, tough fibrous connective tissue, allowing zero movement so that the delicate brain is protected. The shoulder is a freely movable (synovial) ball-and-socket joint with a joint cavity, synovial fluid, an articular capsule and a synovial membrane, allowing rotational movement in multiple planes so that the arm can be used for mechanical work.
why: **Describe the immovable joint.** Immovable (fibrous) joints, such as the sutures of the skull, are bound together by dense, tough fibrous connective tissue and allow zero movement.
**State the advantage of the immovable joint.** Because no movement is possible, the fused skull bones form a rigid protective case for the delicate tissues of the brain.

**Describe the freely movable joint.** The shoulder is a freely movable (synovial) joint: the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with lubricating synovial fluid, enclosed by an articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane.

**State the mechanical advantage and conclude.** The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, so a ball-like head fits into a cup-like socket and rotational movement in multiple planes is possible. This gives the arm a wide range of movement for lifting and manipulating objects, whereas the skull sutures give protection instead of mobility.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A long-distance bus driver in Keren complains of stiffness and pain in his back. Explain how the type of joint between the vertebrae allows the spine to be both flexible and shock-absorbing, and contrast this with the joint that allows the head to turn from side to side.
questions.answer: The vertebrae are joined by slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints separated by fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs, which permit limited, restricted movement so the spine is flexible and the discs absorb shock. The side-to-side turning of the head is produced by the pivot joint between the atlas and the axis, which allows rotation around a central axis.
why: **Identify the joint between the vertebrae.** The 33 vertebrae are separated by fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs, making these slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints that are connected by resilient pads of cartilage.
**Explain the movement and shock absorption.** Slightly movable joints permit only limited, restricted movement; this gives the spine flexibility while the discs absorb shock and provide stability.

**Identify the joint used for turning the head.** The first two cervical vertebrae form the atlas-axis joint, which is a pivot joint in which a rounded surface rotates within a ring, allowing rotation around a central axis.

**Contrast the two joint types and conclude.** The vertebral joints are cartilaginous and allow only slight movement distributed along the column, whereas the atlas-axis pivot joint allows full rotation of the head. Neither joint is a freely movable synovial joint of the ball-and-socket kind.

questions.q: A 13-year-old student in Keren is told by a doctor that the long bones of her arms and legs are still elongating. (a) Explain how endochondral ossification at the epiphyseal plates allows a long bone to increase in length, naming the cells and processes involved. (b) Explain why elongation stops at skeletal maturity. (c) The unit states that approximately 10% of the entire adult skeleton is completely replaced every year by bone remodeling. Deduce the number of years required for a complete turnover of the skeleton, and name the two cell types responsible for remodeling and state the role of each.
questions.answer: (a) The embryonic cartilage model is invaded by blood vessels that deliver osteoblasts, which replace cartilage with mineralised bone, while at the epiphyseal plate chondrocytes divide on the cartilage side and osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone elongates. (b) Elongation stops because the epiphyseal plates completely ossify at skeletal maturity, leaving no cartilage to be converted into bone. (c) A complete turnover of the skeleton takes $$\frac{100\%}{10\%} = 10\text{ years}$$; the two cell types are osteoblasts (which build and mineralise bone matrix) and osteoclasts (which dissolve bone minerals and digest collagen, releasing calcium).
why: **State the starting material of the embryonic skeleton.** During early fetal development the skeleton is composed almost entirely of flexible hyaline cartilage, and ossification is the process by which this embryonic cartilage is transformed into solid bone.

**Describe endochondral ossification.** In endochondral ossification, blood vessels invade the cartilage models and deliver osteoblasts, which gradually replace the cartilage with a hard mineralised matrix.

**Explain growth at the epiphyseal plate.** In children the epiphyseal plates (growth plates) lie between the shaft and the ends of long bones. Chondrocytes continuously divide on the cartilage side of the plate, while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone elongates.

**Explain why growth stops at skeletal maturity.** The plates continue to allow elongation only until they completely ossify at skeletal maturity. Once the plate has ossified there is no cartilage left for the chondrocytes to divide and for the osteoblasts to replace, so the bone can no longer increase in length.
**Calculate the time for complete skeletal turnover.** If 10% of the skeleton is replaced each year, then the time for a complete turnover is $$\frac{100\%}{10\%\text{ per year}} = 10\text{ years}$$.

**Name the remodeling cells and their roles.** Osteoblasts are bone-building cells that synthesise and deposit the organic osteoid matrix and facilitate its mineralisation. Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated bone-resorbing cells that secrete acids and enzymes to dissolve bone minerals and digest collagen, releasing calcium into the blood.

questions.q: A 15-year-old boy in Massawa fractures the shaft of his femur while playing football, and the doctor says the bone will heal rapidly. Explain why bone heals much faster than cartilage following physical trauma, referring to the blood supply and cells of each tissue.
questions.answer: Bone heals rapidly because it is highly vascular: the periosteum is rich in blood vessels and contains bone-forming osteoblasts, and the central canals and perforating canals deliver nutrients and cells directly to the injury site. Cartilage is entirely avascular and must rely on slow nutrient diffusion from the surrounding perichondrium, so it heals much more slowly.
why: **Describe the blood supply and cells of bone.** The unit states that the outer surface of a bone is covered by the periosteum, a fibrous membrane rich in blood vessels, nerves and bone-forming stem cells called osteoblasts, and that central canals and perforating canals carry vessels into the bone.

**Link this to rapid repair.** Because nutrients and osteoblasts are delivered directly to the fracture site by the rich blood supply, the bone matrix can be rebuilt quickly, which is why a fractured femur shaft heals rapidly.

**Describe the blood supply of cartilage.** Cartilage is entirely avascular (lacking blood vessels), so it must rely on slow nutrient diffusion from the surrounding tissues (perichondrium) to repair itself.

**Conclude the comparison.** The absence of a direct blood supply makes cartilage repair slow, whereas the highly vascular periosteum, central canals and perforating canals of bone make bone repair comparatively rapid.

questions.q: A child in Asmara suffers a disorder in which the epiphyseal plates of the long bones ossify completely at the age of 8 years instead of at skeletal maturity. Predict the effect on the length of the child's arms and legs, and explain the role of the growth plate in normal bone elongation, naming the cells involved.
questions.answer: The arms and legs will stop elongating at 8 years and the child will remain unusually short, because the epiphyseal plates have ossified and no cartilage remains. Normally chondrocytes divide on the cartilage side of the plate while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone keeps elongating until the plate ossifies at skeletal maturity.
why: **Recall the normal role of the epiphyseal plate.** The epiphyseal plates (growth plates) lie between the shaft and the ends of long bones; chondrocytes continuously divide on the cartilage side of the plate while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side.
**Relate the plate to elongation.** This continuous division and replacement is what allows bones to elongate during childhood, so the arms and legs grow longer year by year.

**Apply the premature ossification.** If the plates ossify completely at 8 years, there is no cartilage left for chondrocytes to divide and no cartilage for osteoblasts to replace, so elongation of the long bones ceases permanently.

**State the predicted outcome.** The child's arms and legs will stop growing at 8 years and remain short, so the child will be unusually short, whereas normally elongation continues until the plates ossify at skeletal maturity.

body: **A muscle** is a body structure that is made up of fibrous tissue.
A complete muscle contains bundles of muscle fibres.

Smooth muscle cells are fusiform (spindle-shaped) with a single central nucleus and lack repeating sarcomeres, making them non-striated.

Therefore, the correct choice is **It is composed of spindle-shaped cells, lacks striations, and is involuntary.**

cards.title: Antagonistic pair: biceps and triceps
body: To bend the arm the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes. To straighten it the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes.

cards.title: Step by step: Voluntary (skeletal) muscles
body: **Step 1:** Voluntary muscles are attached to bones by tendons and are controlled consciously by the nervous system; under a microscope they are striated (striped) and multinucleated.
**Step 2:** A muscle can only pull (contract); it cannot push.
**Step 3:** So muscles work in antagonistic pairs: when one contracts, the other relaxes.
**Step 4:** The origin is the end attached to a fixed bone; the insertion is the end attached to the bone that moves.
**Step 5:** The flexor bends a joint (biceps at the elbow); the extensor straightens it (triceps).
**Example:** Bending the arm: biceps contracts (shortens), triceps relaxes, the forearm is pulled up. Straightening the arm: triceps contracts, biceps relaxes, the forearm is pulled down.

cards.q: Which of the following describes the relationship between the biceps brachii and triceps brachii during forearm flexion?

options.A: Both muscles contract simultaneously as synergists.
options.B: The biceps brachii acts as the agonist (flexor) while the triceps brachii acts as the antagonist (extensor) and relaxes.
options.C: The triceps brachii acts as the agonist while the biceps brachii relaxes.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze forearm flexion mechanics**
Bending the arm at the elbow joint is flexion, which decreases the joint angle.

**Step 2: Map to agonist and antagonist roles**
The biceps brachii is the flexor (agonist) and contracts. The triceps brachii is the extensor (antagonist) and must relax and stretch.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **The biceps brachii acts as the agonist (flexor) while the triceps brachii acts as the antagonist (extensor) and relaxes.**

cards.q: The Descending Loop of Henle is highly permeable to which of the following substances?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review transport features of the Loop of Henle**
The Loop of Henle has structurally asymmetric limbs with differing permeabilities.

**Step 2: Identify descending limb properties**
The descending limb is highly permeable to water but virtually impermeable to solutes (like sodium and urea), allowing water to enter the hypertonic medulla via osmosis.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Water**.

cards.q: Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) regulates water reabsorption by binding to receptors on cells of which nephron segment?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify hormone action site**
While most water is reabsorbed passively in the $$PCT$$, facultative (regulated) water reabsorption occurs in the final segments of the nephron.

**Step 2: Match with ADH target**
$$ADH$$ targets the cells of the collecting ducts (and to a lesser extent, the distal tubules), stimulating them to insert aquaporins for water reabsorption.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Collecting Duct**.

cards.title: Homeostasis and negative feedback
body: **Homeostasis** is keeping the internal environment (temperature, water, glucose, pH) nearly constant. It works by **negative feedback**: a change from the normal level is detected by receptors, a control centre (often the brain or a gland) sends a message, and an effector brings the level back to normal. Example: when body temperature rises, sweating and widening of skin blood vessels cool the body down.

cards.title: 5.2.1 Structure of the Mammalian Kidney
body: **The kidneys** are a pair of vital organs that perform a variety of functions.
Every day, a person’s kidneys process approximately 189 litres of blood and filters out about two litres of waste products and excess water.
The waste and excess water becomes urine, which flows to the urinary bladder through tubes called ureters.
The urinary bladder stores urine until releasing it through urination.

cards.title: 5.2.2 Osmoregulation by the Kidney
body: **Osmoregulation** is the process which regulates the concentration and osmotic pressure of blood by regulating the water contents of blood plasma.

The human kidney is extremely flexible in handling different types of activities.

cards.title: Step by step: Control of water balance (osmoregulation)
body: **Step 1:** Osmoregulation keeps the water content and solute concentration of the blood constant.
**Step 2:** Each kidney has about a million nephrons: blood is filtered at the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule (ultrafiltration).
**Step 3:** Useful substances (all glucose, most water and salts) are reabsorbed in the tubule; water is reabsorbed especially in the collecting duct.
**Step 4:** The hypothalamus detects blood concentration; the pituitary gland releases ADH (antidiuretic hormone). ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable, so more water returns to the blood.
**Step 5:** Negative feedback: when blood becomes normal again, ADH secretion falls back.

**Example:** On a hot day in Massawa you sweat a lot and drink little: blood becomes concentrated → more ADH → more water reabsorbed → small volume of dark, concentrated urine. After drinking lots of water: less ADH → large volume of pale, dilute urine.

cards.title: Glucose
body: High sugar → insulin → liver stores glycogen. Low sugar → glucagon → liver releases glucose. (Same islets as Unit 1 — the book wants you to connect them.)

cards.title: 5.3.1 The Pancreas and its Hormones
body: The pancreas secretes the hormones insulin and glucagon to control the level of glucose in the blood.
The body of a healthy person, who has not eaten for some time, releases a small amount of insulin into the bloodstream throughout the day and night.
Maintaining this steady supply of insulin is important in allowing the body to utilize blood sugar for a longer period after a meal.
The insulin also sends signal to the liver to convert glucose into the glucosereserve known as glycogen.

cards.title: 5.3.2 The Liver and Sugar Control
body: The liver acts as a storehouse for glycogen.

Insulin - Insulin is released as a result of an increase in glucose levels, and stimulates the liver to convert glucose into glycogen, where the excess glucose can be stored for later use in the liver.
Insulin also signals the liver when more glucose is needed.
If a person has exhausted his/her glycogen stores, as can happen on a low carbohydrate intake, the liver converts fats or protein into glucose to provide the glucose the body needs.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which pancreatic hormone is secreted in response to hypoglycemia (low blood glucose), and what is its primary effect?

options.B: Glucagon; raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis
options.D: Insulin; raises blood glucose by storing glycogen

cards.why:
**Step 1: Differentiate pancreatic hormones**
Insulin is secreted during hyperglycemia (high blood sugar). Glucagon is secreted during hypoglycemia (low blood sugar).

**Step 2: Define glucagon function**
Glucagon directs the liver to perform glycogenolysis (breaking down glycogen to release glucose), raising blood glucose back to normal.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Glucagon; raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis**.

cards.title: Control of blood glucose
body: After a meal, glucose rises → the pancreas releases **insulin** → liver and muscles change glucose to **glycogen** and cells take up glucose → level falls. Between meals, glucose falls → the pancreas releases **glucagon** → the liver changes glycogen back to glucose → level rises again. Both hormones act by negative feedback.

cards.title: Temperature — skin
body: Hot: sweat + vasodilation (skin red) + hair down. Cold: shiver (muscle heat) + vasoconstriction + hair up (little use in humans). Hypothalamus is the thermostat.

cards.title: 5.4.1 The Structure of Human Skin
body: One of the major organs for regulating the temperature is the skin.
The skin has a very large surface area and is in direct contact with the external environment.
The skin is divided into two layers: the outer epidermis and inner dermis.
**The malpighian layer** is the boundary between these two layers.

cards.title: 5.4.2 Mechanisms of Heat Loss
body: All mammals and birds maintain a constant body temperature despite the change in the temperature of the environment.
The temperature of the body is regulated by feedback mechanisms which operate primarily through the hypothalamus.
The hypothalamus contains not only the control mechanisms, but also the key temperature sensors.
A rise in body temperature is compensated for by increasing heat loss and reducing heat production.

cards.title: 5.4.3 Mechanisms of Heat Gain
body: The heat production of the body under a normal temperature range remains almost constant.
The effectors for this response are the body’s skeletal muscles, which contract and relax involuntarily to generate heat.
The capillaries in the skin become constricted.
Hair-erection: When the body is cold, the muscles attached to the hair follicles contract.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: How does cutaneous vasodilation assist in cooling the human body in a hot environment?

options.A: It diverts blood inward to deep abdominal organs to decrease metabolic rates.
options.B: It widens dermal blood vessels, bringing warm blood close to the skin surface to maximize heat loss via radiation and convection.
options.C: It constricts superficial capillaries to decrease sweating.
options.D: It increases the thickness of the insulating subcutaneous fat layer.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand vasodilation mechanics**
Vasodilation refers to the relaxation of smooth muscles in blood vessel walls, increasing their diameter.

**Step 2: Analyze thermal heat exchange**
Widening dermal blood vessels increases blood flow to the skin, allowing core heat carried by blood to be lost to the external environment through radiation and convection.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **It widens dermal blood vessels, bringing warm blood close to the skin surface to maximize heat loss via radiation and convection.**

options.A: Voluntary movement designed to increase blood flow to the skin surface
options.B: Involuntary, synchronous contractions of skeletal muscles to release thermal energy as a byproduct of ATP hydrolysis
options.C: Autonomic stimulation of sweat glands to produce insulating fluids

cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify shivering tissue**
Shivering involves skeletal muscles, which are normally voluntary but act involuntarily under hypothalamic control during cold stress.

**Step 2: Describe energy conversion**
Rapid, synchronous contractions hydrolyze $$ATP$$. Since muscle contraction is only partially efficient, a large portion of this energy is released as heat to warm the body.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Involuntary, synchronous contractions of skeletal muscles to release thermal energy as a byproduct of ATP hydrolysis**.

units.title: Plant Systems
units.intro:
**Growth** = irreversible increase in size; **development** = new organs (leaf, flower). Seeds may stay dormant until water, warmth and oxygen arrive.

**Plant hormones:** auxin (tip → elongate cells, phototropism), gibberellin (stem / germination), cytokinin (cell division), ethene (ripening), abscisic acid (dormancy / stomatal close in drought).

f4.title: Root hair zone drinks; stem holds xylem/phloem; leaf is the factory; flower is the sex kit.

cards.title: Mnemonic — A.G.C.E.A.
body: Auxin Grows, Cytokinin Divides, Ethene Ripens, ABA Sleeps. (Two A’s: Auxin and Abscisic acid.)

cards.title: 6.1.1 Growth and Development in Flowering Plants
body: In plants growing points are found at the tip of stems and roots.
In special circumstances the young (immature) cells of a root, stem or leaf may become active and divide to form a new root or a new shoot.
Leaves have limited growth which determines their size and shape.
Young cells in the leaf-bud divide repeatedly to give rise to the leaf tissue.

cards.title: 6.1.2 Seed Dormancy and Germination
body: Dormant seeds are seeds which remain viable (alive) though metabolically inactive and incapable of germination under the conditions normally favourable for the species.
In other words, the seed is “asleep”, waiting for the ideal conditions to awaken.
**Seed dormancy** is a mechanism that ensures the survival of the species.
Dormancy enables the plant to avoid periods of environmental stress such as dry season or cold winter temperatures.

cards.title: 6.1.3 Plant growth hormones — chemical messengers of plants
body: **Step 1 — what they are.** Plant hormones are **chemical substances** that affect a plant’s ability to **respond to its environment**. They are usually **made in one part** of the plant and **transported to another** where they act — just like animal hormones, but plants have no glands; growing tips, young leaves, seeds and fruits make them.
**Step 2 — why “growth regulators”.** They can **stimulate or inhibit** growth, so they are also called **plant growth regulators**.
**Step 3 — they act on targets.** They interact with specific **target tissues** to cause responses such as **growth, flowering, fruit ripening, leaf fall or dormancy**.
**Step 4 — teamwork.** Each response is often the result of **two or more hormones acting together** — sometimes helping each other, sometimes opposing (antagonism).

**Step 5 — the five groups:** **auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and abscisic acid (ABA).** The first three mostly **promote** growth; ABA mostly **inhibits**; ethylene **ripens** fruit and speeds leaf fall.

cards.title: The five plant hormones at a glance
head: Hormone

NAA roots cuttings; more tomato fruits; 2,4-D weed killer

cards.title: Auxins — the elongation and bending hormone
body: **The natural auxin** is **indoleacetic acid (IAA)**, produced in the **apical meristem of the shoot**, in actively growing shoot tips and in developing fruits.
**Main job — cell elongation.** IAA makes cells just behind the tip **stretch**, so the shoot grows longer.
**Phototropism (bending to light):** when light comes from one side, auxin collects on the **shaded side**; cells there elongate **more**, so the shoot **curves towards the light**.
**Geotropism:** auxin also redistributes under gravity, helping shoots grow up and roots grow down.

**Apical dominance:** auxin from the terminal bud **inhibits the lateral (side) buds**, so an intact plant grows tall with few branches. Remove the tip and the side buds grow — the plant becomes **bushy**.
**Other effects:** inhibits **abscission** (leaf/fruit fall), promotes **fruit development**, stimulates **root initiation**, and helps **cell division** and growth.

steps.text: **The tip makes auxin**, which moves down the shoot.
**Light from one side** → auxin moves to the **shaded side**.
**Shaded-side cells elongate more** → the shoot bends towards the light.

cards.title: Apical dominance — why pruning makes a plant bushy

steps.text: **Intact plant:** auxin from the terminal bud flows down and holds back the lateral buds → tall, few branches.
**Tip removed (pruned):** no auxin from the top → lateral buds grow → bushy plant. Gardeners “pinch out” tips of hedges, tea and tomato plants for this reason.

cards.title: Synthetic auxins — chemistry on the farm
body: **What:** cheap compounds made by chemists with structures **similar to IAA**.
**NAA (naphthalene acetic acid):** used to **promote root formation** in stem and leaf cuttings (rooting powder) — useful for propagating roses, coffee, grapevines.
**Fruit set:** gardeners spray auxins on **tomato** plants to **increase the number of fruits** on each plant.

**2,4-D — a selective herbicide (weed killer):** it **kills dicots** (broad-leaved weeds such as dandelion and pigweed) **without injuring monocots** (lawn grasses and cereals such as wheat, barley, maize, sorghum and teff). The dicot weeds grow so fast and abnormally that they die.

cards.title: Gibberellins — the “grow taller” hormone
body: **Main effect:** **stimulate the elongation of stems.** Spraying a plant with gibberellins usually makes it grow **taller than normal**. (Dwarf varieties often make little gibberellin.)

**Other effects:** stimulate **lateral buds**, **seed germination** (they switch on enzymes that digest the seed’s food store), **fruit development**, cell division and elongation; they **inhibit root initiation** (the opposite of auxin).
**Use:** sprayed on **grapes** to **increase fruit size** and the **distance between fruits** (less crowding, less rot).

cards.title: Cytokinins — the cell-division hormone
body: **Main effect:** **promote cell division** (cyto = cell, kinesis = division).
**Other effects:** stimulate **lateral buds**, **seed germination** and **cell elongation**; (they also delay ageing of leaves — extra).
**Tissue culture:** cytokinins are very important when plant tissue is grown in the laboratory. The **ratio of auxin to cytokinin** in the medium decides what the tissue makes.

cards.title: Abscisic acid (ABA) and ethylene — the “stop” and “ripen” hormones
body: **ABA generally inhibits other hormones**, such as the auxin IAA. It was first thought to cause **abscission** (leaf fall) — hence its name — but botanists now know that **ethylene is the main abscission hormone**.

**ABA and dormancy:** ABA brings about **dormancy in buds** (e.g. before a dry season) and **maintains dormancy in seeds**, so they do not germinate at the wrong time. (In drought it also closes stomata to save water.)
**Ethylene** is responsible for **fruit ripening** — softening, sweetening (starch → sugar) and colour change. With ABA it speeds the **abscission** of leaves and fruits.
**The odd one out:** unlike the other four, **ethylene is a gas** at room temperature, so it spreads through the air from one fruit to another — “one ripe fruit ripens the basket”.

cards.title: Memory hook — one verb per hormone: “All Good Cooks Ask Eggs”
body: Read the first letters in textbook order: Auxin, Gibberellin, Cytokinin, ABA, Ethylene.

letters.m: Aims the shoot at light (elongation, bending)

cards.title: Traps examiners love (6.1.3)
body: **Abscisic acid is NOT the main abscission hormone** — ethylene is. ABA = dormancy/inhibition.
**Ethylene is the only gas.**
**Auxin inhibits lateral buds; cytokinin stimulates them.**
**Root initiation:** auxin promotes, gibberellin inhibits.
**Tissue culture:** high auxin → roots; low auxin (high cytokinin) → shoots.
**2,4-D kills dicots** (broad leaves), not monocots (grasses, cereals).

cards.title: Activity 6.3 — guavas and a ripe banana
cards.problem: Unripe guavas were sealed in bags alone (bags 1–4) or with a ripe banana (bags 5–8). After 2–3 days the cut guavas were tested with iodine. Describe the expected observations and explain them.

steps.text: Step 1: Identify the variable — the only difference is the **ripe banana**; bags 1–4 are the control.
Step 2: Observation — guavas with a banana turn **yellow, soften and smell sweet sooner**; control guavas stay greener and harder.
Step 3: Iodine test — control guavas stain **blue-black strongly** (much starch); test guavas stain **less** (starch has changed to sugar).
Step 4: Explanation — the ripe banana gives off **ethylene gas**; in a sealed bag it builds up and **speeds ripening** of the guava, which converts starch to sugars.
Step 5: Conclusion — ethylene is a gaseous hormone that ripens fruit; this is why one ripe fruit can ripen others nearby.

cards.answer: Guavas with a banana ripen faster and show less starch (weaker blue-black) because the banana releases ethylene gas, which promotes ripening.

cards.title: Apply it — weeds in a wheat field
cards.problem: A farmer near Mendefera sprays 2,4-D on a wheat field full of broad-leaved weeds. Predict and explain the result.

steps.text: Step 1: Wheat is a **monocot**; broad-leaved weeds are **dicots**.
Step 2: 2,4-D is a synthetic auxin that is **selective** — it kills dicots but not monocots.
Step 3: The weeds grow abnormally and die; the wheat is unharmed and gets more water, light and minerals.

cards.answer: The broad-leaved (dicot) weeds die while the wheat (monocot) survives, so the crop yield increases.

cards.title: Apply it — making a bushy hedge
cards.problem: A gardener wants a thick, bushy hedge. What should she do, and which hormone explains it?

steps.text: Step 1: The terminal bud makes **auxin**, which suppresses lateral buds (apical dominance).
Step 2: Cutting off the shoot tips removes this auxin source.
Step 3: Lateral buds now grow into side branches → bushy hedge.

cards.answer: Trim (pinch out) the shoot tips regularly; removing the auxin source ends apical dominance so side branches grow.

cards.title: Apply it — tissue culture
cards.problem: In a tissue-culture lab, a piece of potato tissue produced many roots but no shoots. How should the medium be changed to get shoots?

steps.text: Step 1: Many roots → the medium has a **high auxin : cytokinin ratio**.
Step 2: Shoots need a **low** ratio.
Step 3: So reduce auxin and/or add more cytokinin.

cards.answer: Lower the auxin-to-cytokinin ratio (more cytokinin, less auxin).

**Step 2:** Ethylene is a gas at room temperature.

cards.title: Step by step: Plant tissues
body: **Step 1:** Meristematic tissue: small, dividing cells at root and shoot tips (apical meristems – growth in length) and in the cambium (lateral meristem – growth in thickness).

**Step 2:** Permanent simple tissues: parenchyma (thin-walled living cells for storage and photosynthesis), collenchyma (unevenly thickened living cells for flexible support in young stems) and sclerenchyma (dead cells with lignified walls for rigid support – fibres and stone cells).
**Step 3:** Complex tissues: xylem (vessels and tracheids – carry water and minerals up, dead, lignified) and phloem (sieve tubes and companion cells – carry sugars both ways, living).
**Step 4:** Dermal tissue: epidermis with a waxy cuticle, stomata and root hairs.
**Step 5:** These tissues form three tissue systems: dermal, vascular and ground.
**Example:** Why can a young sunflower stem bend in the wind without breaking? Collenchyma gives flexible support; later, as the stem thickens, sclerenchyma and xylem give rigid support.

lessons.title: The Root: Primary Structure and Function

cards.title: Tissues
body: Meristem (divides), parenchyma (pack), collenchyma / sclerenchyma (support), xylem (water up, dead tubes), phloem (sugar both ways, living).

cards.title: Root hair zone drinks; stem holds xylem/phloem; leaf is the factory; flower is the sex kit.
Tissues
body: Root systems: tap (one main, e.g. carrot) vs fibrous (grass). Regions: cap, division, elongation, hair/maturation. Leaf: cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade (photosynthesis), spongy + stomata (gas).

cards.title: 6.3.1 Tap and Fibrous Root Systems
body: The two principal functions of roots are the absorption of water and minerals, and anchorage.
When the seed germinates, the radicle is usually the first structure to appear; it becomes the first root and is called the **primary root**.
In many plants (e.g. beet, radish and carrot), the primary root remains the principal root throughout the life of the plant.
The development of a fibrous root system (like that of barley or wheat) is different from that of a tap root system.

cards.title: 6.3.2 Root growth regions — four zones behind the root tip
body: **Step 1 — the big picture.** A young root grows in length only at its **tip**. A long section of the tip shows **four regions** (from the tip upwards): **root cap → region of cell division → region of elongation → region of maturation**.
**Step 2 — not walls, but a gradient.** The regions are **not strictly separate**: cells made in one region gradually develop into those of the next as the tip moves on.

**Step 3 — follow one cell.** A cell is made by division just behind the cap, then **stretches** in the elongation zone, then **specialises** (e.g. into a root-hair cell or a xylem vessel) in the maturation zone. So reading the zones from tip to top is like watching a cell’s life story.

cards.title: The root tip, region by region

steps.text: **Root cap** — cup of parenchyma cells protecting the delicate tip; outer cells are worn away by soil.
**Region of cell division** — meristem; small cube-shaped cells with large nuclei, few tiny vacuoles; makes all root tissues and new cap cells.
**Region of elongation** — cells take in lots of water and grow long; small vacuoles merge into one or two large ones (up to 90 % of the cell).
**Region of maturation (differentiation, root-hair zone)** — cells become permanent tissues; root hairs absorb most water and minerals.

cards.title: Root cap and region of cell division
body: **Root cap:** made of **parenchyma** cells forming an **inverted cup** over the tip of each root. Its outer part is **rough and uneven** because cells are constantly **worn away** as the root pushes through the soil. **Main function: protect the delicate root tip** (the meristem). (Extra: its cells make slimy mucilage that eases the way and they sense gravity.)

**Where new cap cells come from:** the textbook says the cap “arises from cells in the region of elongation”, but in the next paragraph it states correctly that the **growing point (region of cell division) gives rise to new root cap cells**. Use the second statement in exams: **the meristem replaces the worn cap cells**.

**Region of cell division:** the zone **next to the root cap**, made of **actively dividing meristematic cells** from which **all other root tissues** are formed. Cells are **cube-shaped**, with **fairly large nuclei** and **few, if any, small vacuoles** — typical of cells that spend their energy dividing.

cards.title: Region of elongation and region of maturation
body: **Region of elongation:** immediately behind the growing point. Cells become **longer and somewhat wider**, remain **undifferentiated**, and grow rapidly by **taking in large quantities of water**. The tiny vacuoles **merge into one or two large vacuoles** that may fill **90 % or more** of the cell. This zone **pushes the tip forward** through the soil.

**Why growth stops above it:** only the **root cap and apical meristem actually move** through the soil, so there is **no further increase in length above the region of elongation** — older parts are anchored.

**Region of maturation** (also **region of differentiation** or **root-hair zone**): cells **mature and differentiate** into the **permanent tissues** — epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, xylem, phloem.

**Root hairs:** each is a **slender lateral projection of a single epidermal cell**. The **cuticle is very thin** here. Any epidermal cell can absorb, but root hairs give a **much larger surface**, so **most water and minerals enter through root hairs**. They are **short-lived**: they wither as the root grows and new ones form nearer the tip.

cards.title: Experiment — where does a root grow?
cards.problem: A germinating bean root is marked with ink lines 1 mm apart, starting at the tip. After 24 hours the spacing is measured. Predict and explain the result.

steps.text: Step 1: Lines on the cap stay close; the cap only moves forward.
Step 2: Lines about 2–5 mm behind the tip become **widely spaced** — this is the **region of elongation**, where cells stretch.
Step 3: Lines further back (maturation zone) stay **1 mm apart** — no more growth there.
Step 4: Conclusion: growth in length happens in a short zone just behind the tip.

cards.answer: Marks just behind the tip (elongation zone) spread apart most; marks further back do not move apart, showing growth happens only near the tip.

cards.title: Exercise 6.3 Q1, Q2 and Q4
cards.problem: (1) What are the regions of root development? (2) What is the function of the root cap? (4) Describe the region of cell maturation.

steps.text: Step 1 (Q1): Root cap, region of cell division, region of elongation, region of maturation.
Step 2 (Q2): The root cap protects the delicate root tip (meristem) as it pushes through the soil; its worn cells are replaced from the meristem.

Step 3 (Q4): In the maturation (root-hair) zone cells differentiate into permanent tissues; epidermal cells grow root hairs with a thin cuticle that absorb most water and minerals; the hairs are short-lived.

cards.answer: (1) Root cap, region of cell division, region of elongation, region of maturation. (2) It protects the delicate root tip as the root pushes through the soil. (4) Cells differentiate into permanent tissues; epidermal cells form short-lived root hairs with a thin cuticle that absorb most water and minerals.

cards.title: Apply it — transplanting seedlings
cards.problem: Why should seedlings be transplanted with a ball of soil round their roots?

steps.text: Step 1: Most water is absorbed by delicate **root hairs** near the tip.
Step 2: Pulling a seedling out bare tears off the root hairs.
Step 3: With few root hairs the plant cannot absorb enough water and wilts; keeping soil round the roots protects them.

cards.answer: To avoid damaging the root hairs, which absorb most of the water and minerals.

cards.title: Traps examiners love (6.3.2)
body: **Growth in length = elongation zone**, not the division zone (division makes cells; elongation makes the root longer).
**Root hairs are in the maturation zone**, not at the very tip.
**A root hair is one cell**, not many.
**Vacuoles:** tiny in the division zone, huge in the elongation zone.

cards.q: Cells with large nuclei and almost no vacuoles are found in the
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Large nucleus + no vacuole = dividing cell.

**Step 2:** That is the meristem (region of cell division).

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A root hair is

options.B: a projection of a single epidermal cell

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Root hairs grow from epidermal cells.

**Step 2:** Each hair is an outgrowth of one cell.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In which root tip region do cells undergo rapid increase in length by absorbing large quantities of water?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** “Increase in length by absorbing water” describes cells that stretch.

**Step 2:** Cap = protection; division = making cells; maturation = specialising.

**Step 3:** Stretching happens in the zone of elongation, where small vacuoles merge into large ones.

**Answer: C.**

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: In which root tip region do cells undergo rapid increase in length by absorbing large quantities of water?

steps.text: Step 1: Recall the four regions from the tip: cap, division, elongation, maturation.
Step 2: Match each to its job — protect, divide, stretch, specialise.
Step 3: “Increase in length by taking in water” = stretch → elongation.
Step 4: Check: vacuoles grow to 90 % of the cell in this zone.

cards.title: 6.3.3 Internal Structure of the Root
body: In cross section, a root has an epidermis, cortex, endodermis and pericycle, and xylem and phloem.
**The cortex** is the tissue immediately inside the epidermis and functions in storing food.
The innermost layer of the cortex is the endodermis.
Inside the endodermis is a cylinder of parenchyma cells called the pericycle.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the primary function of Abscisic Acid (ABA) in plants during environmental stress?

options.A: To promote rapid stem elongation and leaf growth
options.B: To accelerate fruit ripening and flower opening
options.C: To maintain seed dormancy and trigger rapid stomatal closure during water deficit
options.D: To stimulate cell division in lateral buds

cards.why:
**Step 1: Define ABA as a stress hormone**
$$ABA$$ is synthesized in plastids and acts as a key stress signaler.

**Step 2: Connect with water conservation**
Under drought stress, $$ABA$$ causes potassium ions to exit guard cells, closing stomata to prevent transpiration water loss, and maintains seed dormancy.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **To maintain seed dormancy and trigger rapid stomatal closure during water deficit**.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify root vascular layers**
Water absorbed by roots passes through the epidermis and cortex toward the vascular cylinder.

**Step 2: Identify the regulatory barrier**
The endodermis is the innermost cortical layer. Its cell walls contain suberin (the Casparian strip), which blocks apoplastic water flow, forcing water to pass through cell membranes to regulate mineral entry.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Endodermis**.

lessons.title: The Shoot: Primary Structure and Function

cards.title: 6.4 The shoot — stem, leaves and flowers
body: **The shoot system** is everything above the ground: **stems, leaves and flowers**. The stem is the frame and pipeline, the leaves are the food factories, and the flowers are the reproductive organs.
**Order of this lesson:** 6.4.1 stem → 6.4.2 leaf → 6.4.3 flower, each with external structure, internal structure and functions.

cards.title: 6.4.1 The stem — functions and external structure
body: **Four functions of the stem:** (i) it **bears the leaves**; (ii) holds them where they get **plenty of light**; (iii) **conducts** water and minerals up to the leaves and manufactured food from the leaves to other parts; (iv) in some plants it **stores food** (e.g. potato tuber, sugar cane).
**What a stem is:** an **axis** with leaves attached and a **growing point at the tip**. The tip is protected by overlapping young leaves forming the **terminal bud**.
**Leaf arrangement:** **alternate** (one leaf per node, on alternate sides), **opposite** (two per node, facing each other) or **whorled** (three or more per node).
**Nodes and internodes:** a **node** is where a leaf attaches; the stretch between two nodes is the **internode**.

**Axil and axillary bud:** the angle between a leaf and the stem is the **axil**; the bud in it is the **axillary bud** (the textbook calls the angle itself the axillary bud). Axillary buds grow into **new branches or flowers**.

cards.title: External features of a stem
head: Feature
Meaning
Why it matters
rows: Growing tip covered by young leaves
Distinguishes a stem from a root
Spaces leaves so they do not shade each other
Angle above a leaf / bud in it

cards.title: Internal structure of a young dicot stem (sunflower)
body: A thin transverse section seen under the microscope shows **four regions, from outside to centre**:
**a. Epidermis** — **one cell thick**; outer walls thickened with **cutin**, forming a waterproof **cuticle** that stops water loss and keeps out gases and germs.
**b. Cortex** — just inside the epidermis, outside the conducting tissue; **parenchyma** cells with **large intercellular spaces** (for gas exchange and storage).

**c. Vascular bundles** — arranged in a **ring**. Each has **phloem** on the outside (carries **manufactured food** from leaves to other parts) and **xylem** on the inside (carries **water and minerals** from roots to leaves). Between them, **cambium** cells divide constantly to make **new phloem and xylem**, so the stem can grow thicker.
**d. Pith** — the **centre**; the **most extensive tissue**, of **parenchyma** with the **largest cells** in the section; stores food and water.

steps.text: **Dicot (sunflower):** bundles in a **ring**, cambium between xylem and phloem, cortex outside the ring, large pith in the centre.
**Monocot (maize):** bundles **scattered** throughout, **no cambium**, **no distinct pith**, very little cortex.

cards.title: Memory hook — outside to centre: “Every Cat Visits Paris”
body: Exercise 6.4 Q1 asks exactly this order.

cards.title: Exercise 6.4 Q1
cards.problem: List the pattern of tissues in a young dicot stem from the outside to the centre.

steps.text: Step 1: Outermost — epidermis (with cuticle).
Step 2: Then cortex (parenchyma).
Step 3: Then the ring of vascular bundles — phloem, cambium, xylem (outside → inside).
Step 4: Centre — pith.

cards.answer: Epidermis → cortex → vascular bundles (phloem, cambium, xylem) → pith.

cards.title: Apply it — ring-barking a tree
cards.problem: Goats strip a complete ring of bark from a young tree. The leaves stay green for weeks, but the tree later dies. Explain.

steps.text: Step 1: Bark includes the **phloem**, which lies outside the xylem.
Step 2: The xylem (inside) is untouched, so water still reaches the leaves — they stay green.
Step 3: Food made in the leaves cannot pass the ring through phloem to the roots.
Step 4: The roots starve, stop absorbing, and the whole tree dies.

cards.answer: Removing the ring removes the phloem: water still rises in the xylem, but food can no longer reach the roots, which die, and then the tree dies.

cards.title: Activity 6.8 — identify the slide
cards.problem: A slide of a stem section shows vascular bundles scattered all over, with no central pith. Is it a dicot or a monocot? Give two reasons.

steps.text: Step 1: Scattered bundles → monocot.
Step 2: No pith → monocot.
Step 3: Check for cambium — absent in monocots.

cards.answer: Monocot — scattered bundles, no pith (and no cambium).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which tissue carries manufactured food from the leaves to other parts?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Xylem = water and minerals up.

**Step 2:** Phloem = food from leaves.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The part of a stem between two nodes is the
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Node = where a leaf joins.

**Step 2:** Between two nodes = internode.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: 6.4.2 The leaf — the food factory: external structure
body: **Job:** the leaf is the **site of food production**. Here the plant takes in **light energy** and **carbon dioxide** for photosynthesis and **releases oxygen**.
**Monocot vs dicot leaves:** monocots typically have **simple leaves with parallel venation**; dicots have **branching (net) venation** and many shapes.
**Three parts of a typical dicot leaf:**
**① Blade (lamina)** — the flat, extended part. Its edge is the **margin**: **toothed** in sunflower, **smooth** in bean. **Veins** run through it carrying water and nutrients.
**② Petiole** — the short stalk attaching the leaf to the stem; it continues into the centre of the lamina as the **midrib**.
**③ Leaf base** — the point of attachment. Some leaves have **stipules** (small scale-like or leaf-like outgrowths) at the base; in most monocots the base widens into a **sheath** around the stem.

cards.title: Internal structure of the leaf — layer by layer
body: **Upper epidermis:** a **single layer** of closely fitting, comparatively large, water-filled cells, covered by a **thick waxy cuticle** that reduces water loss. Cells are **transparent**, so light passes through.
**Palisade layer (upper mesophyll):** **2–3 layers** of **long, cylindrical** cells packed with **many chloroplasts** — the main photosynthetic tissue, placed where light is strongest.
**Spongy layer (lower mesophyll):** **loosely packed** cells in a network with **many air spaces**; they also contain chloroplasts. The air spaces let gases diffuse through the leaf.
**Veins (vascular bundles):** continuous with those of the stem — **xylem** brings water and minerals; **phloem** takes food away. They also support the blade.

**Lower epidermis:** a single layer of **small cells** with **very numerous stomata** between them. Each stoma is a pore between two guard cells. (In some plants stomata occur on both surfaces; in others only on the lower surface.)
**Stomata** control **water loss** and allow **free diffusion of CO₂ and O₂**.

cards.title: Leaf transverse section — top to bottom

steps.text: **Cuticle** — waxy, waterproof layer.
**Upper epidermis** — one layer, clear, no gaps.
**Palisade mesophyll** — tall cells crammed with chloroplasts.
**Spongy mesophyll** — loose cells, big air spaces.
**Vein** — xylem (water in) and phloem (food out).
**Lower epidermis with stomata** — gas exchange.

cards.title: Leaf layers and their jobs (Exercise 6.4 Q2)
head: Layer
Structure
Function
rows: 2–3 rows of long cells, many chloroplasts
Loose cells, air spaces, some chloroplasts

cards.title: Gas exchange through the stomata — step by step (Activity 6.9)
body: **Step 1:** In light, photosynthesis uses CO₂, so CO₂ concentration inside the leaf falls.
**Step 2:** CO₂ **diffuses in** through the open **stomata** (mostly on the lower surface) into the **air spaces** of the spongy layer.
**Step 3:** It moves through the air channels to the **palisade cells**, passes through the **wet cell walls** and **dissolves** in the cell sap, reaching the chloroplasts.
**Step 4:** **Oxygen** made by photosynthesis diffuses the opposite way and out through the stomata.
**Step 5:** Water vapour also escapes through open stomata (**transpiration**). Stomata **close at night** or in drought, saving water but stopping CO₂ entry.

cards.title: From glucose to starch
body: **Photosynthesis:** in sunlight, **water and carbon dioxide react inside the chloroplast** to form **glucose** (and oxygen). The flat, expanded leaf gives a **large surface area** — the best shape for absorbing light.

**Storage:** glucose is **removed from the cell sap quickly** and turned into **insoluble starch**, stored as small solid **starch grains** in the chloroplasts. Insoluble starch does not upset the water balance (osmosis) of the cell.

**Note on “leucoplasts”:** the textbook says starch is deposited “in the form of leucoplasts”. Leucoplasts are actually **colourless plastids that store starch in non-green parts** (e.g. potato tubers, roots); in the leaf itself, starch grains lie **inside the chloroplasts**.

cards.title: How the leaf is adapted for photosynthesis
head: Feature
How it helps
rows: Large surface to absorb light and CO₂
Palisade near the top, many chloroplasts
Most chlorophyll where light is strongest
Water in, food out; supports the blade

cards.title: Memory hook — top to bottom: “Clever Unicorns Prefer Sweet Vanilla Lollipops”
body: Cuticle, Upper epidermis, Palisade, Spongy, Vein, Lower epidermis.

cards.title: Exercise 6.4 Q2
cards.problem: Name the different tissue layers of a leaf.

steps.text: Step 1: Start at the top — cuticle on the upper epidermis.
Step 2: Mesophyll — palisade layer then spongy layer, with veins (vascular bundles) running through.
Step 3: Bottom — lower epidermis with stomata.

cards.answer: Upper epidermis (with cuticle), palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll (with vascular bundles/veins), lower epidermis (with stomata).

cards.title: Explain — why most stomata are on the lower surface
cards.problem: Why do many plants have more stomata on the lower surface of the leaf?

steps.text: Step 1: The upper surface faces the sun and is hotter.
Step 2: Stomata there would lose much more water by evaporation.
Step 3: On the shaded, cooler lower surface water loss is less, while CO₂ can still enter the air spaces of the spongy layer just above.

cards.answer: To reduce water loss: the lower surface is cooler and shaded, yet still opens directly into the spongy air spaces.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The main photosynthetic tissue of a leaf is the
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Photosynthesis needs chloroplasts and light.

**Step 2:** The palisade layer is near the top and packed with chloroplasts.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The petiole continues into the lamina as the
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The petiole is the leaf stalk.

**Step 2:** It runs up the centre of the blade as the midrib.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: 6.4.3 The flower — structure
body: **What a flower is:** the part of the shoot **specially modified for reproduction**. It sits on a **flower stalk (pedicel)** whose swollen tip is the **receptacle**.

**Four whorls (rings) of floral parts**, from the **outside towards the centre**: **calyx (sepals) → corolla (petals) → androecium (stamens) → gynoecium (pistil/carpels)**. (The textbook lists gynoecium before androecium; in a real flower the **stamens form a ring outside the central pistil**.)
**Calyx:** the outermost whorl of **sepals** — modified leaves that **protect the flower in the bud**; usually green, sometimes brightly coloured.
**Corolla:** the **petals** — often brightly coloured and scented to **attract insects** (pollinators); they may be **joined into a tube** or **free**.
**Androecium (male):** the **stamens**. Each stamen = a **filament** (stalk) supporting an **anther** (sac containing **pollen grains**).

**Gynoecium (female):** one or more **pistils (carpels)**. Each pistil = **stigma** (flattened or branched top with a **sticky surface** that catches pollen) + **style** (stalk joining stigma to ovary) + **ovary** (enlarged base housing the **ovules**).

cards.title: Flower long section — the four whorls

steps.text: **Calyx — sepals:** protect the bud.
**Corolla — petals:** attract pollinators.
**Androecium — stamens** (filament + anther): make pollen.
**Gynoecium — pistil** (stigma + style + ovary): receives pollen; ovules inside.

cards.title: Floral whorls
head: Whorl
Made of
Function
rows: Catch pollen; contain ovules; become fruit

cards.title: Describing flowers and plants — six terms
body: **Complete flower:** has all four parts (sepals, petals, stamens, pistil). **Incomplete:** one or more missing.
**Essential parts** are the **stamens and pistil** (they make the gametes).
**Perfect (bisexual) flower:** has **both** stamens and pistil (e.g. bean, hibiscus). **Imperfect (unisexual):** has **only one** of them.
**Monoecious plant** (“one house”): **separate male and female flowers on the same plant** — e.g. **maize** (tassel = male, cob = female), **pumpkin**.
**Dioecious plant** (“two houses”): **male and female flowers on different plants** — e.g. **papaya**; a farmer needs at least one male tree near the female trees to get fruit.

cards.title: Flower and plant terms (Exercise 6.4 Q5 b, c)
head: Pair
First term
Second term
rows: Male + female flowers on one plant (maize, pumpkin)
Male and female flowers on separate plants (papaya)

cards.title: Function of the flower — pollination
body: **Main function:** produce **male and female gametes** and bring them together. The **pollen grains** (which carry the male gametes) are made in the **anthers**; the **ovules** (which contain the egg) are made inside the **ovary**.
**Pollination** = the **transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma** of a flower of the **same kind (species)**.
**Self-pollination:** pollen goes to the stigma of the **same flower** or **another flower on the same plant**.

**Cross-pollination:** pollen goes to the stigma of a flower on **another plant** (of the same species) — carried by insects, wind, birds or water. It mixes genes from two parents, giving **more variation**.

cards.title: Fertilization and double fertilization — step by step
body: **Step 1 — germination of pollen.** Pollen landing on the stigma is nourished by a **sticky (sugary) substance** and **germinates**, growing a **pollen tube**.

**Step 2 — two nuclei become three.** A pollen grain has a **generative nucleus** and a **tube nucleus**. The generative nucleus divides into **two male nuclei**. The tube nucleus and the two male nuclei travel down the tube **within the style**.
**Step 3 — reaching the ovule.** The tube grows to the **ovary**, enters the **ovule through the micropyle**, and its tip **bursts**, releasing the two male nuclei.
**Step 4 — inside the ovule (embryo sac):** an **egg nucleus**, **two polar nuclei**, **three antipodal cells** and **two synergids**.
**Step 5 — fusion one:** one male nucleus + **egg nucleus** → **zygote** (grows into the embryo).
**Step 6 — fusion two:** the second male nucleus + the **two polar nuclei** → **endosperm** nucleus (grows into the food store of the seed).
**Step 7 — name it:** two fusions at once = **double fertilization**, found **only in flowering plants**.
**Step 8 — after fertilization:** petals, stamens and style **wither**; the **ovule becomes the seed** and the **ovary becomes the fruit**.

steps.text: **Pollen tube** grows down the style and enters the ovule through the micropyle, carrying two male nuclei.
**Male nucleus 1 + egg → zygote** (2n) → embryo.
**Male nucleus 2 + two polar nuclei → endosperm** (3n, extra detail) → food store.

cards.title: Memory hook — whorls outside → in: “Some People Sing Professionally”
body: Sepals, Petals, Stamens, Pistil — and remember **STAMEN has “MEN” = male**.

cards.title: Traps examiners love (6.4.3)
body: **Pollination ≠ fertilization.** Pollination moves pollen; fertilization fuses nuclei.
**Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit.** Students often swap them.
**Double fertilization:** egg + male nucleus = zygote; two polar nuclei + male nucleus = endosperm.
**Monoecious = one plant has both kinds of flower**; dioecious = separate male and female plants.
**Stamens lie outside the pistil** in the flower.

cards.title: Exercise 6.4 Q3 and Q4
cards.problem: (3) What are the components of the stamen and the pistil? (4) Which parts of the flower give rise to a seed and to a fruit?

steps.text: Step 1 (Q3): Stamen = filament + anther (with pollen).
Step 2 (Q3): Pistil = stigma + style + ovary (with ovules).
Step 3 (Q4): After double fertilization the ovule develops into the seed.
Step 4 (Q4): The ovary enlarges into the fruit.

cards.answer: Stamen: filament and anther. Pistil: stigma, style and ovary. Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit.

cards.title: Exercise 6.4 Q5
cards.problem: Distinguish: (a) self- and cross-pollination; (b) perfect and imperfect flowers; (c) monoecious and dioecious plants.

steps.text: Step 1 (a): Self — pollen to a stigma of the same flower or same plant; cross — to a flower on another plant of the same species.
Step 2 (b): Perfect — has both stamens and pistil; imperfect — has only one of them.
Step 3 (c): Monoecious — male and female flowers on the same plant (maize); dioecious — on different plants (papaya).

cards.answer: (a) Self: pollen to the same flower/plant; cross: to another plant of the same species. (b) Perfect: both stamens and pistil; imperfect: only one. (c) Monoecious: male and female flowers on one plant (maize); dioecious: on separate plants (papaya).

cards.title: Apply it — a lonely papaya tree
cards.problem: A farmer plants one papaya tree. It flowers every year but never bears fruit. Explain and advise.

steps.text: Step 1: Papaya is **dioecious** — male and female flowers are on different trees.
Step 2: If the tree is male it can never fruit; if female, it has no pollen source nearby.
Step 3: Without pollination there is no fertilization, so no ovary becomes a fruit.
Step 4: Advice — plant several trees, including at least one male, near the female trees.

cards.answer: Papaya is dioecious; the single tree cannot be pollinated (or is male). Plant male and female trees together.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which part of the pistil catches pollen?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The pistil = stigma, style, ovary.

**Step 2:** The sticky stigma catches pollen.

**Answer: C.**

cards.why:
**Step 1:** First male nucleus + egg = zygote.

**Step 2:** Second male nucleus + two polar nuclei = endosperm.

**Answer: B.**

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Separate male and female flowers → imperfect flowers.

**Step 2:** Both on one plant → monoecious.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which leaf mesophyll layer consists of tightly packed, vertically elongated cells optimized for capturing sunlight for photosynthesis?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze leaf internal anatomy**
The leaf interior (mesophyll) is divided into palisade and spongy layers.

**Step 2: Match with photosynthetic specialization**
The palisade mesophyll is located on the upper surface, consisting of tightly packed, columnar cells rich in chloroplasts to maximize solar energy capture.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Palisade mesophyll**.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze leaf internal anatomy**
The leaf interior (mesophyll) is divided into palisade and spongy layers.
**Step 2: Match with photosynthetic specialization**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In between upper and lower epidermis of the leaf section, there are palisade layer and spongy layer, both collectively known as____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Identify leaf layers. A typical leaf has a protective outer epidermis.
**Step 2:** Identify the internal tissue. The ground tissue located between the two epidermal layers is called the **mesophyll**.
**Step 3:** Sub-divide the mesophyll. It is usually differentiated into the **palisade mesophyll** (column-like cells for photosynthesis) and **spongy mesophyll** (loose cells for gas exchange).
**Step 4:** Conclusion. Collectively, they form the mesophyll layer.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In a dicot stem, the vascular bundles are arranged:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Dicot stems have vascular bundles arranged in a ring, with cambium between xylem and phloem.

**Step 2:** Monocot stems have scattered vascular bundles and no cambium.

**Step 3:** Answer: in a ring.

**Tip:** The cambium in the ring lets dicot stems grow thicker (secondary growth).

cards.title: 6.5 Transport Systems in Plants
body: Soil water is absorbed by the root hairs.
Once the water enters a root hair it passes from one cell to another by osmosis until it reaches the xylem.
Water in the xylem moves up from the roots to the stem and leaves by the action of root pressure and transpiration pull.
Root pressure is one of the forces that push water up the xylem.
The pulling force set up by the evaporation of water from the leaves is called **transpiration pull**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following describes the double fertilization event in angiosperms?

options.A: Two sperm cells fertilize two separate egg cells to produce fraternal twins.
options.B: One sperm fertilizes the egg to form a zygote, while the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.
options.C: One sperm fertilizes the ovary wall, while the second sperm forms the seed coat.
options.D: Two pollen tubes fertilize the same egg to produce a diploid endosperm.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Review angiosperm reproductive events**
Angiosperms undergo a unique double fertilization process utilizing two sperm nuclei from a single pollen tube.

**Step 2: Trace both fertilization pathways**
One sperm ($$n$$) fertilizes the egg ($$n$$) to form a zygote ($$2n$$). The second sperm ($$n$$) fuses with the two polar nuclei ($$n+n$$) to form the triploid endosperm ($$3n$$).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **One sperm fertilizes the egg to form a zygote, while the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.**

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Which of the following describes the double fertilization event in angiosperms?

**Step 2: Trace both fertilization pathways**

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **One sperm fertilizes the egg to form a zygote, while the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.**

cards.answer: One sperm fertilizes the egg to form a zygote, while the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which theory explains the upward transport of water through xylem vessels based on transpiration pull, molecular attraction, and water tension?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review water transport models**
Water moves up tall plants under negative pressure (tension).

**Step 2: Name the primary model**
The cohesion-tension theory explains that water is pulled up by transpiration, held together by hydrogen bonds (cohesion), and supported by xylem walls (adhesion).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Cohesion-tension theory**.

**Step 2: Name the primary model**

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Cohesion-tension theory**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Sugars made in the leaves are carried to other parts of the plant through the ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Xylem carries water and minerals upward from the roots.

**Step 2:** Phloem carries dissolved sugars (translocation) from leaves to roots, fruits and growing points.

**Step 3:** So sugars move in the phloem.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

glossary.meaning: The male part of a flower: all the stamens, which produce pollen.
Plant hormones that make cells elongate; they control phototropism and geotropism.
The palisade layer is the upper region of the mesophyll consisting of two or three layers of long, cylindrical cells.
Simple plant tissue of thin-walled living cells, used for storage, photosynthesis and packing.
A layer of cells just inside the endodermis of a root from which lateral roots grow.
The cortex is the tissue immediately inside the epidermis and functions in storing food.
Living plant tissue that carries dissolved sugars and other food from the leaves to other parts.
The outermost whorl of a flower, made of the sepals, which protect the bud.
Seed dormancy is a mechanism that ensures the survival of the species.
The innermost layer of the root cortex; it controls the movement of water and minerals into the vascular tissue.

tips.text: Growth is the sum total of various processes that result in an irreversible increase in mass, weight, and volume.
Plant growth occurs by cell division, elongation and differentiation.
In plants growing points are found at the tips of stem and roots.
The tissues in these growing tips are called meristems.
Growth consists of an increase in the number of cells and increase in cellular components.
The resting stage of a seed in which growth is halted and metabolism reduced is called seed dormancy.
Germination is the starting of the growth process of a plant embryo.
Seed germination depends on both internal and external conditions.
The most important external factors are water, oxygen and suitable temperature.

Growth hormones are compounds that promote, inhibit, or otherwise modify growth, development and differentiation in plants. There are five major groups of plant hormones: auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and abscisic acid.

questions.q: Which of the following is a simple plant tissue?
why: **Simple tissues** are composed of only one type of cell. Examples include **Parenchyma**, Collenchyma, and Sclerenchyma. Xylem and Phloem are **complex tissues** because they consist of multiple cell types.

questions.q: The absorption of water by seeds is known as_______.
why:
**Step 1:** Define the terms.
- Transpiration: Loss of water vapor from leaves.
- Micropyle: Small opening in the seed coat.
- **Imbibition:** The physical process of water absorption by dry seeds, which causes them to swell and triggers germination.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: All of the following are correct, except

options.A: abscisic acid are inhibits other hormones
options.B: cytokinins promote cell division in plants
options.C: ethylene is responsible for the ripening of fruit
options.D: auxins influence the stimulation of seed germination

why:
**Step 1:** Review plant hormone functions.
- A is correct: ABA is a stress hormone and growth inhibitor.
- B is correct: Cytokinins promote cytokinesis (cell division).
- C is correct: Ethylene gas triggers fruit ripening.
**Step 2:** Evaluate D. While auxins influence many growth processes, **Gibberellins** are the primary hormones responsible for stimulating seed germination. High levels of auxins can actually inhibit germination in some cases.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: During germination, seeds absorb water through the
why: The micropyle is a tiny pore in the seed coat (testa). Its primary function is to allow water to enter the seed to initiate germination (imbibition).

questions.q: Which of the following is true about inhibitors in seed dormancy?

options.C: they are found in food storage tissue
options.D: they are found in outer covering of the seed or fruit

why:
**Step 1:** Understand seed dormancy. Dormancy is a state that prevents seeds from germinating even under favorable conditions.
**Step 2:** Identify chemical inhibitors. Hormones like Abscisic Acid (ABA) act as inhibitors.
**Step 3:** Locate these inhibitors. They can be found in various parts of the seed or fruit, including the endosperm, cotyledons, storage tissues, and the seed coat (outer covering) to prevent premature germination.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Which of the following hormone is responsible for ripening of fruits?
why:
**Logic:**
- **Cytokinin:** Cell division.
- **Auxin:** Cell elongation.
- **Ethylene:** A gaseous hormone that triggers **fruit ripening** and leaf fall.
- **Gibberellin:** Stem growth.
- **Abscisic Acid:** Inhibits growth (stress hormone).

**Result:**
Ethylene.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Meristematic tissues are

options.A: are absent on the tips of a stem.
options.B: are absent on the tips of a root.
options.C: have no capacity of continuous division.
options.D: are absent on the tips of leaves.

why: **Meristematic tissues** are specialized for continuous cell division and are found at the growing tips of roots and stems (apical meristems). They are generally not found at the tips of leaves, making D the correct factual statement among the choices.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: A group of plants with out specialized vascular cells are ______?
why:
**Step 1: Define vascular plants.**
Vascular plants have xylem and phloem to transport water and nutrients.

**Step 2: Categorize the options.**
- **Ferns, Pines, Beans:** All are vascular plants.
- **Mosses (Bryophytes):** Non-vascular plants that lack specialized conducting tissues.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Identify the plant hormone that initiates the conversion of starch in fruits into sugar?
why: Ethylene is the gaseous plant hormone responsible for fruit ripening. During ripening, it triggers enzymes that break down complex starches into simple sugars, making the fruit sweet.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Seed germination normally does not depend on
why: Seed germination requires water (to soften the seed coat), oxygen (for aerobic respiration to provide energy), and a suitable temperature. **Carbon dioxide** is needed for photosynthesis, but since a germinating seed hasn't grown leaves yet, it doesn't need CO2 to start growing.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Explain how auxin causes a shoot to bend towards light.
questions.answer: Auxin is made in the shoot tip. When light comes from one side, auxin moves to the shaded side. Cells on the shaded side elongate more than those on the lit side, so the shoot curves towards the light (positive phototropism).
why: Step 1: source — tip.
Step 2: redistribution to the shaded side.
Step 3: unequal elongation.
Step 4: bending to light.
questions.tip: Keep the order: tip → shade → stretch → bend.

similar.q: What would happen if the tip were covered with a foil cap?

Step 2: ethylene is a gas, spreads.
Step 3: ventilation + cold slow ripening.

similar.a: Permanent tissues such as xylem, phloem, cortex and endodermis.

why: Step 1: root hairs are short-lived.
Step 2: they wither as the root grows and new ones form nearer the tip → false.
questions.tip: Root hairs are temporary.

similar.a: Old ones die; new hairs are needed to keep absorbing water in fresh soil.

questions.q: Explain why there is no further increase in root length above the region of elongation.
questions.answer: Only the root cap and the apical meristem actually move forward through the soil. Cells above the elongation zone have stopped stretching and become differentiated; they are fixed in the soil (often by root hairs), so that part of the root does not lengthen.
why: Step 1: what moves — cap and meristem.
Step 2: cells above have finished elongating.
Step 3: they differentiate and are anchored.
questions.tip: Growth in length = only the tip region.

similar.q: Which region produces new cells for root growth?
similar.a: The region of cell division (apical meristem).

questions.q: State one structural feature and the function of each of the four root regions.
questions.answer: Root cap — cup of parenchyma cells, protects the tip. Cell division — small cube-shaped cells with large nuclei, make new cells. Elongation — cells with large vacuoles, increase root length. Maturation — root hairs and differentiated tissues, absorb water and minerals.
why: Step 1: cap.
Step 2: division.
Step 3: elongation.
Step 4: maturation.

Step 2: the meristem divides and adds cells to the cap.
Step 3: elongating cells only stretch; they do not divide.
questions.tip: Only dividing (meristem) cells can make new cells.

Step 2: xylem intact → leaves get water.
Step 3: roots get no food → die.
Step 4: tree dies.

Step 2: air spaces.
Step 3: wet cell wall — dissolves.

questions.q: Name the three parts of a typical dicot leaf and state the function of the petiole.
questions.answer: Blade (lamina), petiole and leaf base. The petiole attaches the leaf to the stem, holds the blade out towards the light and carries the vascular tissue (continuing as the midrib).
why: Step 1: three parts.
Step 2: petiole role.
questions.tip: Lamina–petiole–base, top to bottom.

similar.q: What is a stipule?
similar.a: A small scale-like or leaf-like outgrowth at the base of some leaves.

questions.label: 6.4.3 Practice — the flower

questions.q: Describe double fertilization in flowering plants.
questions.answer: The pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and releases two male nuclei. One male nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus to form the zygote, which becomes the embryo; the second fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the endosperm, the food store. Two fusions occur, so it is called double fertilization; it is found only in flowering plants.
why: Step 1: pollen tube delivers two male nuclei.
Step 2: fusion 1 → zygote.
Step 3: fusion 2 → endosperm.
Step 4: name and uniqueness.
questions.tip: Count the fusions: two.

questions.label: 6.4.3 Practice — the flower

questions.q: Distinguish between pollination and fertilization.
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma of a flower of the same species. Fertilization is the fusion of a male nucleus with the egg nucleus (and, in flowering plants, another male nucleus with the polar nuclei) inside the ovule. Pollination comes first.
why: Step 1: define pollination.
Step 2: define fertilization.
Step 3: order.
questions.tip: Pollination moves pollen; fertilization fuses nuclei.

why: Step 1: the pollen grain has a tube nucleus and a generative nucleus.
Step 2: the tube nucleus is associated with growth of the tube; the generative nucleus makes two male nuclei.
questions.tip: Tube nucleus → tube.

questions.label: 6.4.3 Practice — the flower

questions.q: Why do insect-pollinated flowers usually have large, brightly coloured, scented petals?
questions.answer: The petals (corolla) attract insect pollinators by their colour and scent. Insects visiting for nectar pick up pollen from the anthers and carry it to the stigma of another flower, bringing about (cross-)pollination.
why: Step 1: role of petals — attraction.
Step 2: insects move pollen.
Step 3: result — pollination.
questions.tip: Structure → attraction → pollination.
